PRIVILEGE-MR. LAWSON POWERS OP CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION RESPECTING OPERATION AND CONTROL OF STATIONS
speechtext:
I rise to a question of privilege. Speaking in the house on Tuesday on the amendment to the address in reply to the speech from the throne, with regard to the powers of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, I made a statement which, in an interruption by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Howe), was alleged to be erroneous; and subsequently, at the end of my speech, the minister said that my statement was wrong and that I should admit it.
I claim the privilege of quoting to the house the authority upon which I base my statement; that authority is the Canadian Broadcasting Act. If you will refer to page 263 of Hansard, Mr. Speaker, you will find that I used these words:

Privy Council Appeals-Mr. Cahan
May I Bay to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Howe) that I understood the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation not only operates stations but controls all stations in Canada.
The minister said:	-
The hon. member is entirely wrong.
I tried in a hurry to locate the provisions in the act but was unable to do so, and the Minister of Transport, immediately upon the conclusion of my address, as shown at page 266, said:
What the hon. member stated is not the fact; why not say so?
I quote from the Canadian Broadcasting Act, being chapter 24 of the statutes of Canada for the year 1936, section 22:
The corporation may make regulations:
(b)	to prescribe the periods to be reserved periodically by any private station for the broadcasting of programs of the corporation.
This was a program of the corporation, that was in question.
(c)	to control the character of any and all programs broadcast by corporation or private stations.
I say, therefore, Mr. Speaker, that my statement was correct. It was correct also on a further ground; the broadcast in question was a chain broadcast. A private station cannot obtain wires for the conduct of a chain broadcast without application to the commission under section 22, subsection 1(a), and therefore the commission has control of the private stations.

subtopic: PROPOSED ABOLITION OF APPEALS TO HIS MAJESTY IN COUNCIL

speechtext:
Hon. C. H. CAHAN (St. Lawrence-St. George) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 19, respecting appeals to the judicial committee of the privy council.
He said: In moving for leave to introduce this bill, which is entitled An Act Respecting Appeals to the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council, I would ask the privilege of
making a few explanatory remarks, not by way of argument but for the purpose of enabling lay members of the house to appreciate more clearly the development of the constitutional law with respect to prerogative appeals to his majesty in council and with respect to the appeal under the statutory provision of a later act to the judicial committee of the privy council.
A statute of the parliament of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland, which was enacted in 1833 and is best known by its short title, The Judicial Committee Act, 1833, recites the fact that "from the decisions of various courts of judicature in the East Indies and in the plantations, colonies and other dominions of his majesty abroad, an appeal lies to his majesty in council," and proceeds by its provisions to regulate the proceedings in such an appeal. But under the Judicial Committee Act, 1833, it was never claimed that as a matter of royal prerogative the king and his privy council had jurisdiction to review the judgments of a colonial court, other than from the final appellate court in the colony, which, in the British American provinces, was the governor and his executive council.
The first royal commission appointing a governor of a province in that part of British North America now known as the Dominion of Canada was the commission issued in 1749 to Edward Cornwallis as governor of the newly-created province of Nova Scotia. Upon his arrival at Halifax Cornwallis appointed his council and established three courts for the province; a court of general sessions, similar to courts of sessions in England, a county court of five justices of the peace having jurisdiction over the entire province, and a general court consisting of the governor and members of his council, having a supreme appellate jurisdiction in the province. This supreme court of the governor in council exercised both political and judicial functions. The right of appeal to the governor in council was omitted from the royal instructions to the governors of Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island in 1861.
In 1754 Jonathan Belcher was appointed chief justice of the province of Nova Scotia, and chief justice of the supreme court of judicature, which was then constituted. This court thereafter exercised the appellate jurisdiction that formerly appertained to the governor in council.
The royal proclamation of October 7, 1763, established a judicial system in Quebec, consisting of civil and criminal courts, with a right of appeal in civil cases to the king in council. The Quebec Act, 1774, repealed all existing ordinances relating to the administra-

Privy Council Appeals-Mr. Cahan
tion of justice, but the instructions to Governor Carleton in 1775 authorized the constitution of criminal and civil courts, with an appeal in civil matters to the governor in council in certain cases.
The Constitutional Act of 1791 provided for the division of the old province of Quebec into two new provinces to be called Upper and Lower Canada, and provided that all existing laws, statutes and ordinances should remain in force until altered by the legislatures of the new provinces. The respective legislatures of the two new provinces each enacted statutes making provision for appeals to the governor in council, with a further provision for appeals to the king in council. Lower Canada legislated by 34 George III, chapter 6, section 23. Upper Canada legislated by 34 George III, chapter 2, section 33, which reads as follows:
And be it enacted that the governor, lieutenant governor, or person administering the government of this province, or the chief justice of the province, together with any two or more members of the executive council of the province, shall compose a court of appeal for hearing and determining all appeals from such judgments or sentences as may lawfully be brought before them.
One of the grievances most bitterly complained of in the province of Lower Canada was this constitution of the governor in council as a court of error and appeal, inasmuch as the governor in council exercised, in practice, political rather than judicial functions.
In 1841 the appeal In re Samuel Cambridge from Prince Edward Island was heard before the privy council. By the royal instructions to the governor of that island, then in force, he was directed to allow appeals to himself in council where the value appealed from amounted to £300 sterling and to the king in council where the value appealed from amounted to £500. Cambridge, to avoid a multiplicity of suits against himself, petitioned her majesty in council for leave to appeal from a judgment of the supreme court of the island to the amount of £135 which under the instructions to the governor was not appealable either to the governor in council or to her majesty in council. The judicial committee, Lord Brougham, a former lord chancellor, presiding, held that there being an intermediate court of appeal in the island, namely the governor in council, no appeal could be received by the privy council directly from the supreme court of the island. Appeals from the supreme court of the island under the instructions should be made to the governor in council of the island. The reference is Moore's Privy Council Cases, volume III, page 175. This case was decided in 1841, and thereafter Lord Brougham introduced to

parliament the bill which was enacted as the Judicial Committee Act, 1844, to overcome the difficulty which had arisen, by allowing in future appeals to the privy council from other courts in the colonies although they were not courts of error or courts of appeal.
When this statute was enacted in 1844 the royal instructions to every British governor, without exception, constituted him and his executive council a court of appeal exercising judicial functions as a court of error and appeal, and made further provision for an appeal from the governor in coimcil to the king in his privy council. The Judicial Committee Act of 1844 recites that:
*-the judicial committee, acting under the authority of the said acts-
The act of 1833 and an amending act.
-hath been found to answer well the purposes for which it was so established by parliament, but it is found necessary to improve its proceedings in some respects for the better despatch of business and expedient also to extend its jurisdiction and powers.
The first section of the act of 1844 enacts that it shall be competent to her majesty by general or special order in council to-
-provide for the admission of any appeal or appeals to Her Majesty in council from any judgments, sentences, decrees or orders of any court of justice within any British colony or possession abroad.
The jurisdiction of the king in council to review judgments of colonial courts, other than the final court of appeal where such court existed in the colonies, was never claimed as a matter of royal prerogative prior to the enactment of The Judicial Committee Act, 1844, which converted the pre-existing prerogative right into a statutory right.
The conditions which Lord Brougham desired and intended to remove are shown by the preamble to The Judicial Committee Act, 1844 which recites:
Whereas by the laws now in force in certain of Her Majesty's colonies and possessions abroad no appeals can be brought to Her Majesty in council for the reversal of the judgments, sentences, decrees and orders of any courts of justice wdthin such colonies save only of the courts of error or courts of appeal within the same, and it is expedient that Her Majesty in council should be authorized to provide for the admission of appeals from other courts of justice within such colonies or possessions-
Then it proceeds with the enactment of section 1:
1. It shall be competent to her majesty, by any order or orders to be from time to time for that purpose made with the advice of her privy council, to provide for the admission of any appeal or appeals to her majesty in council

Privy Council Appeals-Mr. Cahan
from the judgments, sentences, decrees or orders of any court of justice within any British oolony or possession abroad, although such court shall not be a court of error or a court of appeal within such colony or possession; and it shall also be competent to her majesty, by any such order or orders as aforesaid to make all such provisions as to her majesty in council shall seem meet for the instituting and prosecuting of any such appeals, and for carrying into effect any such decisions or sentences as her majesty in council shall pronounce thereon.
This statute of 1844, says the late Mr. E. R. Cameron in his valued work on The Canadian Constitution, never contemplated interfering with the power to regulate appeals from the courts of appeal in the provinces of Upper and Lower Canada, given them by the Constitutional Act of 1791. This undoubtedly was the view of the imperial authorities in passing the earlier orders in council which provided for the institution and prosecution of appeals in the Canadian provinces which had no courts of error and appeal other than the governor in council, and which orders are clearly supplementary to the provisions of The Judicial Committee Act, 1844.
The preamble to the orders in council, providing for appeals from New Brunswick in 1852 and Nova Scotia in 1863, recites the language of The Judicial Committee Act, 1844, and proceeds:
And whereas it is expedient that provision should be made in pursuance of the said cited enactments to enable parties to appeal in civil causes from the decision of the supreme court of the province to His Majesty in council, the same not being a court of error and appeal.
When these orders in council of 1852 and 1863 were passed by his majesty in council, each of the provinces of New Brunswick and Nova Scotia was "a British colony or possession" within the meaning and intent of The Judicial Committee Act, 1844; but it may be doubted, I think, whether a province of the Dominion of Canada may now be properly so described. It is clear that in respect of any future enactment of the parliament of the United Kingdom and Northern Ireland it may not be so described, because section 11 of the Statute of Westminster, 1931, provides:
Notwithstanding anything in The Interpretation Act, 1889, the expression "colony" shall not, in any act of the parliament of the United Kingdom passed after the commencement of this act, include a dominion or _ any province or state forming part of a dominion.
In 1849, by 12 Victoria, chapter 37, in Lower Canada, and by 12 Victoria, chapter 63, in Upper Canada, the governor in council as a court of error and appeal was abolished, but provision was made for appeals to the king
in his privy council. Subsequently the thirty, fourth resolution adopted at the Quebec conference in October, 1864, provided that the general parliament should have power to make laws for-
The establishment of a general court of appeal for the federated provinces.
Section 101 of The British North America Act, 1867, subsequently enacted:
101. The parliament of Canada may, notwithstanding anything in this act, from time to time provide for the constitution, maintenance and organization of a general court of appeal for Canada, and for the establishment of any additional courts for the better administration of the laws of Canada.
During the parliamentary session of 1875, which was during the period when this country was administered by the government of Mr. Mackenzie, a bill was introduced by Mr. Fournier, then minister of justice in the Liberal administration of that day, to establish the Supreme Court of Canada. The political records of that time disclose that Edward Blake had a large part in drafting the bill, and that the bill, as originally drawn, contained a clause providing that judgments of the supreme court should be final, thus precluding appeals to the privy council, but that the government of the United Kingdom then intimated to the government of Canada that the proposed act would not receive the assent of the crown unless that section of the bill was amended so as to preserve the prerogative right of appeal. Professor Kennedy, of the university of Toronto, in his work, The Constitution of Canada, at page 341, relates:
When the parliament of Canada in 1875 proceeded to constitute a supreme court for Canada, the bill, as introduced, provided for the cessation of all appeals to the privy council, but the colonial office at London notified the Liberal government of that day that unless this provision was eliminated the whole bill would be disallowed by the government at Westminster.
In May's Constitutional History (1912), volume III, he says that when in 1875 the Liberal government of Canada proposed to abolish appeals to the privy council, the judicial committee prepared a memorandum in which they said:
To abolish this controlling power and abandon each colony and dependency to a separate court of appeal of its own would obviously be to destroy one of the most important ties connecting all parts of the empire in common obedience to the courts of law, and to renounce the last and most essential mode of exercising the authority of the crown over its possessions abroad.
It is to be noted that Canada was then regarded as a colony, dependency or possession of the crown, over which the government of

Privy Council Appeals-Mr. Cahan
the United Kingdom should not renounce the last and most essential mode of exercising authority in the name of and as advisers of his majesty.
The forty-seventh section of the Supreme Court Act of 1875 as then enacted, reads as follows:
47. The judgment of the supreme court shall in all cases be final and conclusive, and no appeal shall be brought from any judgment or order of the supreme court to any court of appeal established by the parliament of Great Britain and Ireland, by which appeals or petitions to her majesty in council may be ordered to be heard; saving any right which her majesty may be graciously pleased to exercise by virtue of her royal prerogative.
That section now appears as section 54 of the Supreme Court Act, chapter 35 of the revised statutes of Canada, 1927.
The parliament of Canada in 1888, by chapter 43 of the statutes of 1888, subsequently enacted amendments to the criminal code, which provided that in criminal cases the judgment of the Supreme Court of Canada should in all cases be final and conclusive, and that no appeal shall be brought in any criminal case to his majesty in council. That remained the law in Canada for thirty-eight years, until, in 1926, in the Nadan case, the privy council held that this enactment of the parliament of Canada was inconsistent with the provisions of the Judicial Committee Acts, 1833 and 1844, and therefore invalid under section 2 of the Colonial Laws Validity Act of 1865, which enacts that:
Any colonial law which is or shall be in any way repugnant to any provisions of any act of parliament extending to the colony to which such law may relate . . . shall to the extent of such repugnancy, but not otherwise, be and remain absolutely void and inoperative.
In the Nadan case it was declared that that enactment in the criminal law of Canada, which presumably had been in force for some thirty-eight years, was invalid and void, by reason of repugnancy to the Colonial Laws Validity Act.
Section 2 of the Statute of Westminster, 1931, has more recently declared that:
The Colonial Laws Validity Act, 1865, shall not apply to any law made after the commencement of this act by the parliament of a dominion.

Hon. J. G. Gardiner,

Mr. Speaker, when the house adjourned last night I was dealing with conditions in the drought area in western Canada, and I had referred to a series of radio addresses and articles in English newspapers by a Mr. A. G. Street with regard to conditions in western Canada. In these articles and addresses Mr. Street lays the blame for conditions in western Canada upon the methods of our farmers there. He says that we were mining the land, taking everything out and putting nothing
back, and that that was the cause of our present conditions. I omitted to say last night, as I intended to say and wish to say now, that if his argument is sound that our conditions are due to our methods of farming, then the older sections of Canada would have no crop and the newer sections would be having crops, because it would be the older sections that would be mined and would run out first. But the very opposite is true. In the older sections of the country, in Manitoba, for example, they are having good crops this year, while in the newer sections, in the southern part of Saskatchewan where I come from, they had no crop. So that our conditions cannot be due to our methods of farming.
I want to deal now with what is being done for the people in the dried-out area, but before entering upon what this government has done. I wish to express my thanks and the thanks of the people of western Canada to all the people in the other sections of this country who, not only last fall but for the past seven or eight yearn, have been giving to us freely and cheerfully of their vegetables and their fruits and products of different kinds in order to help carry our people over the period of depression and crop failures. Our people in western Canada deeply appreciate the generosity of the rest of the people of Canada. We are thankful to them, and we hope the time will soon come when it will not be necessary for us to receive relief from other parts of the country.
I wish also while on this matter to express to this government, and especially to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), the thanks of the people in that district for the carloads of vegetables, fruit, fish, cheese, and beans that were sent out there. It was well received and well distributed-and there was no politics in it, either.
Now I turn to what this government is doing for the people in that area in Saskatchewan. Let me say at the start that for purposes of relief the province of Saskatchewan is divided into two areas. There is, first of all, what we call the one hundred per cent area, consisting of 170 municipalities and several local improvement districts. In that area the federal government pays one hundred per cent of the cost of all the relief. Outside of that area there is a large section of the country on behalf of which this government gives to the province of Saskatchewan, first of all, a grant of one million dollars, to pay for feed and fodder for the people in that district; and they allow the province of Saskatchewan to borrow another million dollars for the same purpose. This govern-
The Address-Mr. Donnelly

ment also gives to Saskatchewan a grant of something like $230,000 a month for taking care of relief in other parts of the province.
I wish to deal particularly with the people in the one hundred per cent area, because that is the district we are concerned with, and it is the district the federal government is specially looking after.
The people in that district are better fed, better clothed and better looked after this year than ever before. I have talked, not to one or two or three but to many men in that district, and invariably they have said to me, one after another, "Doctor, I have more fruit, more vegetables, and more food in my celler with which to feed my family now than. I had in the good years in Saskatchewan. What I say about myself is true of ninety per cent of the people in this district, but they do not want to admit it." Of course there are people who go round finding fault. There are always some people who can never get enough relief. There are also people who go round and carry on an agitation among the people inducing them to complain. Some of these agitators are irresponsible people, but I also know responsible men, men holding public office, men who should not do things of this kind, who have gone throughout the country, stood on public platforms and told the people in that district to sign anything and do anything to get more relief, urging people to be dishonest in order to get relief, and then more and more relief. How can we wonder, then, that there are people who are dissatisfied and who complain that they are not receiving enough relief?
With regard to this relief problem generally, perhaps I had better first outline the methods by which it is administered. The dominion government pa3's one hundred per cent of the relief in the area I have described, and the administration of that relief is entirely in the hands of the provincial government. The provincial government appoints relief inspectors, one for about every five municipalities. The application forms for relief are sent from Regina to the different municipalities, and the municipalities have the relief applicants come into whatever office they designate and make out their applications for relief. These applications, when filled out, are put to one side for the inspection of a committee. A committee is set up, consisting of a relief officer and at least two councillors. In many cases the whole council is on the relief committee. Every one of these relief applications is gone over by this committee. No applicant for

relief can get his relief order increased or decreased or changed in any way except with the consent of this whole committee. Any changes that are made are made by the committee, so if any man's relief order is cut down or increased it is the fault of the committee and of the council, because the council comprises the majority on that committee.
When I hear that there are politics in it, when we are told that people have their relief orders changed because of politics, it is a complete mystery to me how that can happen, and I defy any man in this house or out of it to tell me of one individual in western Canada who has had his relief order changed on account of his political affiliations. No man is asked what his politics are when he applies for relief. There are some C.C.F.-ers and Conservatives in that area, and naturally some of them will slip in on the municipal councils in western Canada, but of course the majority of the people there are Liberals and the majority of our councils are Liberals. These committees are not political machines by any means, and these men are not swayed by politics in the administration of relief. There is no federal politics in it, there is no provincial politics in it. There may be a little municipal politics; sometimes a councillor favours one of his neighbours because he thinks he will vote for him at the next municipal election, or something of that kind. It is said that these relief officers are going around the country building up a great Liberal machine. So far as that is concerned, I have only this to say. I know only one or two relief officers in my constituency, but if I were selecting men to build up a Liberal machine I would choose a far different type of men from these officers; I would look for men who were more effective along the political line and not men who were so favourable to some of my opponents.
Let me now deal for a moment with feed and fodder. Early last summer we realized that there would be a shortage of feed and fodder for stock in the west. The government in its wisdom decided to pay the freight in order to allow the people to ship the cattle out to pasturage. I do not believe that very much of this wras done in my section of the country. We have been doing this for the last four or five years and we have not found it very profitable. Invariably when we have shipped horses or cattle they have come back in the spring poorer than when they went out; a great number of them have died, a great many have never come back. Horses and cattle shipped from that short grass

The Address-Mr. Donnelly
country that I come from, when they go into the north or into Manitoba do not do so well; it takes them a long time to become acclimatized and they do not thrive on the feed they get there. Some of our people last fall shipped cattle into Manitoba. They weighed them before they left and after six weeks the cattle weighed less than they did when they were shipped from Saskatchewan and they had good pasturage. We did not find that practice a good thing. It may be better in other sections of the country, but we did not find it so.
The government, however, put into effect a program whereby they bought cattle and shipped them out of the country, and this is one of the best things it has done for the cattle raisers of the west. I have not heard one complaint with regard to the buying of cattle. There was an independent commission buying cattle, and shipping points were established throughout the province. The cattle raisers were notified when shipments were going to take place and were asked to bring in their stock. Again, some of our agitators went about the country and said to the farmers, "Don't bring in your cattle and offer them to the government; you will have to give them for practically nothing." The result was that some people did not bring in any cattle, and when the shipping day came these people came to town to see what was going on. When they found that the buyers were paying the prices that were actually being paid some of them rushed home and tried to get their cattle into the market. The next week some of them drove across the country, twenty-five, thirty and forty miles, herds of cattle which they sought to market at other shipping points.
Let me give an example of what I know with regard to the price of cattle at that time. One man had a herd for which he said he was willing to take S350. About two weeks after the government initiated this program I saw this man and he told me that he was going to hold his cattle and sell them to the government. I told him I thought he was well advised. About a week before the shipping day a buyer came around and this man took him to his farm. The buyer asked him how much he wanted for his cattle, and the farmer said he would take 8550. The buyer laughed at him, but, pointing to a particular animal, he said he would give $40 for it. The man said he would not take S40 for it. He said, "I will let the hair go with the hide

to the government." The government officials came the week after and bought that stock, and that farmer got, not $350, not $550, but $640 for the lot; and the animal for which he was offered $40 he sold for $62.
I do not know of any man in the whole of my constituency, or anybody in any other part of the province, who was not satisfied with the price received for stock sold to the government buying agency. My hon. friend from Weyburn (Mr. Douglas) referred to a price of $12, $13 or $14 for a milch cow. It must have been many years ago that that was a milch cow; it was one of those canners and cutters. I doubt whether the hon. gentleman would know the difference between a canner and cutter and a milch cow.

of Saskatchewan there have already been purchased 6,500,000 bushels of feed oats; 2,000,000 bushels of barley; 1,250,000 bushels of wheat, and corn and mill feed. All this is ready for shipment. Then we have the coarse feeds. Some people here talk about shipping crews into Manitoba to cut feed. We tried that for a couple of years and found that it was an expensive business. Not only that, but some of our people last fall went from our own municipalities in western Canada to bale hay and feed, but the weather was so wet that they could not make it pay and they came back, not having baled very much. We did find that on account of wet and bad weather in Manitoba and Alberta many farmers there would not leave the cutting of their crops to cut feed, and I do not blame them much. But when I came here and said to hon. members from different parts of Manitoba, "There was lots of feed not cut in your section of the country, lots of hay?" invariably they told me the same thing, that there was no hay worth anything not cut in their districts. They said that any hay that remained uncut they would not haul five miles from the slough to feed any kind of stock. Most of the hay in Manitoba was cut. The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) spoke of seeing burning stacks of straw. Well, Manitoba had quite a lot of straw last year, but much of it was rusted, and a lot was filled with sow thistle. Rusted wheat straw and sow thistle are not very good feed for stock. It was burnt because it was of no value whatever.
Then we had another hon. member speaking about the commission for which the pool offered to look after feed. He mentioned 75 cents; I understood it was 50 cents. That commission was to be paid to the pool on top of the price. The price for No. 1 hay was $8.50 and they wanted 50 cents in addition to that. But in fact there was no commission paid to anyone. No commission has been or is being paid to anybody anywhere to buy hay for western Canada. Three councillors came to me last fall; they wanted to go to Manitoba and bale hay. They wanted to get a baler, and we tried to get one for them. While we were trying, one of them said: " You know, I can get lots of hay in Manitoba, anyway. I have had offers; I have letters here." I asked him what they wanted. He said, " They want $5 to $7.50 a ton." " Have you got the letters?" "Yes." "Well, then, here is fifty cents; send a night letter and order 100 carloads of hay right away." Another man sitting there also said, " Here is fifty cents; send to that other fellow and order 100 carloads right away from him and ask him when he can deliver it and at what

price." We got a wire back next morning saying they did not know when they could deliver, and the price would be $9.50. These were just commission merchants trying to make a little money buying and selling feed. All the feed available in Manitoba and in Alberta has been bought, and we believe that our stock will be well looked after and is being well looked after at the present time.
Now', as to this question of how much stock a man is allowed to keep: the government said, " Tell the people and tell them plainly that this is an emergency measure, that it is only for people who are in need, for people on relief. The government will help a man to keep two or three or four head of stock, or even five, depending upon the size of his family. But if he is able to feed five or six head of stock himself we are not going to give him any feed at all." Some farmers of course said, " I can feed ten or fifteen head of stock, and the government is going to feed five more; so I will keep fifteen or twenty," and they were surprised when the government said, " No, we are not going to give you any feed." Feed was short; why should the government feed stock which a man was able to keep himself? If he was able to keep five or ten or twenty head of stock, he could buy his own feed. It was this misunderstanding that brought about a lot of difficulty.
We have heard a dire tale about animals dying around the country. Well, stock has died in western Canada ever since I have been there, and will continue to die. I investigated a lot of these tales myself. Invariably w'hen I went to the man and asked how old the animal was, he would reply, " Well, eighteen or twenty years." It should have been shot two or three years ago. That is what I found. Some of our United Farmers of Canada lodges, Saskatchewan section, kept writing to the president complaining that unless something was done the stock was all going to die. Mr. Speaker, I share the views expressed by

The Address-Mr. MacNeil
my colleagues in this group as to the inadequacy of the legislative program outlined by the government. At this time I do not intend to state my personal views in regard to the policies under debate; I desire to direct the attention of the house to certain conclusions reached by representative and non-partisan bodies across Canada as to the necessity for definite action by this parliament to deal with the need for low cost and low rental houses.
I believe there is general disappointment that in the speech from the throne there has been no reference to this important subject. Statements previously made by members of the government had given rise to the hope that during the present session some advance might be made to relieve the acute housing shortage and thereby lend impetus to economic recovery. I believe members of all parties would welcome such an advance, and, I am sure, hope that the plans of the government hinted at elsewhere may mature at a very early date. There is an amazing unanimity of opinion everywhere that additional measures can and should be undertaken now by the government to meet this pressing problem. Definite action in this direction would be less costly than further delay. In any event many members must feel, as I feel, that in this house we should lend support to the splendid service rendered by public spirited citizens in many groups across Canada in reference to this problem. I refer particularly to those associated with the National Planning and Housing Association. Their approach to the question has been based wholly on considerations of public welfare. They have brought out the undeniable fact that proper housing is as much a matter of public interest and public welfare as the maintenance of a pure water supply. They have shown that the conditions of a complex industrial society make it impossible for governments to avoid assuming increasing responsibilities to assure to every individual a decent minimum of shelter.
The omission of any reference to this subject in the speech from the throne is all the more significant because of the recommendation contained in the interim report of the National Housing Commission, which report was placed in the hands of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) in July of 1937. The recommendation in connection with housing construction reads in part as follows:
The commission recognized the desirability of a rounding out of governmental housing policy, particularly as regards accommodation for those unable themselves to afford an economic rent-often associated with slum clearance. Action in this field was considered necessary both from the viewpoint of eliminating a social sore all too prevalent, especially

in the larger cities, and because of its effect in stimulating employment in the construction field. This employment stimulus the commission considered would be felt directly, and also indirectly through the impetus that would be given to the Home Improvement Plan and to the Dominion Housing Act.
Again, in another section of the report, the commission states:
In making this recommendation the commission was influenced by the fact that Canadian governmental bodies had expended some $14,000,000 in 1936 to rent accommodation for relief recipients, and that in many instances such accommodation was unsanitary and unsuitable in the extreme. The commission feels that such a situation should not be allowed to continue, in that it breeds conditions tending to increase unemployment by decreasing the employability of numbers of workers, thus making it harder for them to secure employment.	,	. .
The plan recommended by the commission was put before the minister some time after the opening of the parliamentary session of 1937, and it is understood action thereon has been held over. As the government stated on September 10, 1936, that it accepted certain general principles laid down by the commission to govern its intended attack on this important branch of the housing problem, it is hoped that action may shortly prove possible.
In view of the circumstances related in this report it is not unreasonable to expect that the government should take appropriate action this session to implement the recommendations of the commission. It would also seem most unwise to disregard the recommendation on this score of the Canadian federation of mayors and municipalities. This federation represents the local government of more than five millions of the population of the dominion. In the submission of this body to the royal commission on dominion-provincial relations it is recommended:
That the federal government enact a national low rent housing act.
This recommendation was based on the following considerations:
(a)	It has been demonstrated that a substantial proportion of the urban population lives in sub-standard houses and in neighbourhoods that are injurious to health and ^ morals, conducive to delinquency and destructive of family life.	.
(b)	It is also true that private enterprise and local authorities have found no way thus far to provide decent housing for those with low incomes. Competent spokesmen for private enterprise admit that the provision of housing for this social group is beyond their ability. Local authorities are unable to function without financial and other help from the senior governments.
(c)	The provisions of the Dominion Housing Act (1935) are unsuited and inadequate to facilitate a housing program for the low-wage income group.

The Address-Mr. MacNeil
(d)	Therefore, in order that a large proportion of our urban families should not continue to live in unfit dwellings, and to supply the urgent need for housing facilities, conforming to an acceptable minimum standard for the low income groups and thus to attack the serious problems of health, welfare and order, which are directly related to inadequate housing, the municipalities of Canada recommend that:
(1)	A national policy should be adopted for rehousing the low income groups at acceptable minimum standards, as a cooperative undertaking by federal, provincial and local governments, and private enterprise. This policy should be designed to stimulate local initiative, recognize local circumstances, and vest the control, save in exceptional cases, in the local authorities.
(2)	The federal and provincial governments should extend, in accordance with local needs, financial assistance conditioned on the existence of a comprehensive city plan and a housing program meeting satisfactory standards.
(3)	Financial aid should be either in the form of capital grants, long term, low interest loans, or annual rent subsidies.
Here you have the recommendations of practical men who are close to the problem and who have had every opportunity to measure it and to gauge its difficulties.
I submit it is becoming more and more apparent that existing provisions of the Dominion Housing Act, 1935, do not adequately meet the situation. The reasons are obvious.
Here I would say that a good deal of praise is merited by the officials in charge of the administration of the act. They have done much to increase the scope of its usefulness. I do not wish to minimize the value of the pioneering work done, or the importance of plans now under consideration. I believe the information made available with respect to operations under the act indicate definite limitations which exclude the possibility of relieving the housing shortage, or of providing houses for those who need them most.
I wish briefly to touch upon the latest statistics available with regard to operations under the present housing program. The total loans as of December 31, 1937, amounted to 2,150. The total number of family units provided for, by such loans, stood at 3,018, while the total value of loans was $13,034,858.
These statistics should be considered in conjunction with the reports of the construction industry. In 1934 there were 10,135 residential contracts in the dominion, having a total valuation of $30-588,100. In 1936 the number of residential contracts increased to 13,606, with a total valuation of $42,857,900. In 1937 the 18,284 residential contracts had a valuation of $56,207,000. It is true that these statistics indicate an important gain, but when we compare these figures with the estimated
shortage of housing they at once appear pitifully inadequate. It becomes painfully clear that operations under the act do not even touch the fringe of the shortage, and that more extensive measures are sorely needed.
In this connection again we must note the serious backlog in the construction industry. Going back to 1929 we find the total value of construction work stood at $576,651,800. Then, in 1933, at the low point of construction in Canada, the valuation was $97,289,800. In 1936 an increase is indicated to $162,588,000. According to the latest records construction contracts in 1937 were valued at $224,000,000. It may be unwise to attempt to express this backlog in terms of dollars and cents, but there is sufficient to show that it is serious, and that the construction industry is lagging behind all other major national industries in Canada.
In 1931, according to census statistics, there were 2,252,729 households in Canada. In 1937 the number was estimated at 2.350,000. The estimated increase in population since 1931 has been at the rate of 130.000 per year, or 30,000 families per year. It will be seen at once that we are building only about onedhird the number of houses required to keep pace with the growth in population and we are making no adequate provisior for the necessary replacements. It has been reliably estimated that the total shortage of houses in Canada exceeds 300,000. When we consider operations under the act we find that up to December, 1937, the number of loans in British Columbia stood at 253. Vancouver city alone reports a housing shortage of over 12,000. Loans in the province of Quebec totalled 992, while in the city of Montreal 40,000 houses are required to make up the shortage, and that figure does not include the requirements of necessary slum clearance.
Then, there is another phase of the problem with respect to operations under the Dominion Housing Act. The average loan per family unit for the entire period ended December 31, 1937, under the Dominion Housing Act has been $4,319. The lowest average loan for any three-month period during 1937 is shown to be $3,806. Only 756 family units were financed by loans under $3,000. When we face realities with regard to the distribution of income in Canada we realize why the present housing program cannot be expected to serve the needs of those who are now without proper housing facilities. Detailed studies of this phase of the problem have been prepared and published by Mr. H. L. Seymour, planning and housing consultant of this city.
The Address-Mr. MacNeil

It is estimated that in 1935 there was a total income of S3,750,000.000 earned in Canada by 3,800,000 persons receiving wages and salaries, or their equivalent. It is shown that of the gainfully employed:

Certainly it would be better and more constructive to subsidize better housing conditions. While there were approximately 1,000.000 persons on relief, about $135,000,000 was paid out in that year for relief allowances by federal, provincial and municipal authorities. That amounts to about $135 per person, or $620 per family. One will readily see that there were few families on
fMr. MacNeil.]
relief which could pay more than $8 or $12 per month for shelter, and consequently many of these people have been living in dilapidated houses unfit for human habitation. At the same time statistics show that there were
1,750,000	persons in about 385,000 families which had an estimated family income of $620 or less, and an average income of well under $400. A number equal to or greater than the number actually in receipt of relief were receiving incomes as low as or lower than relief standards.
The lesson from this experience is plain. Private enterprise seeking profitable investment at prevailing returns cannot provide decent shelter for the low-wage income group. Professor Urwick of the university of Toronto aptly describes the situation when he states that the economics of the problem are "ridiculously simple." He says further:
The poor have not got decent homes because they cannot pay for them; no one attempts to build better homes for them for exactly the same reason. There is no money in low-cost housing; it is doubtful whether it can ever be low-cost enough. For the present, private enterprise does not come into the picture at all, no sane individual or company would touch the business. So the case for state aid does not need to be proven, it is patent on the surface.
Someone said recently that our society is divided into two classes, those who have more dinners than appetites and those who have more appetites than dinners. The same may be said of the disparities apparent in the housing accommodation of the Canadian people. Some dwell on the sunny side of the fence while the many dwell in the shadows. That which lurks in the shadows threatens the well being of the whole community. I consider that this house has definite responsibilities in this matter which can no longer be evaded.
It is not to our credit that Canada is far behind many other countries in carrying out a housing program. I might refer especially to Sweden, Holland, Belgium and Great Britain. In England and Wales 3.300.000 household units have been constructed from the war up to March, 1937. In proportion to population that is over four times what we have accomplished in Canada. We can learn about housing from Great Britain. We can learn that any stimulus to the building industry is passed on to other industries and has startling and cumulative results. Mr. Herbert N. Casson, writing in Maclean's magazine, has the following observations to make of the results.
British bricklayers are overwhelmed with orders. They have not been able to produce enough. Almost every day, ships come to Britain loaded with brick from Belgium.

The Address

Mr. MacNeil
Many timber merchants have had to double their staffs. Practically every furniture factory is working overtime. Decorators and paperhangers have never in their lives been as busy as they are to-day. Britain is building houses.
And again:
By 1931, a building boom had begun. More than 130,000 houses were built in that year by private builders. Since then the boom has continued. At present it has reached its highest point and is confidently expected to go higher. To any tourist, the most striking feature in Great Britain is the vast number of new houses, and houses in course of construction, most of them on the outskirts of the towns and cities. At last, in spite of a bad start, Britain has succeeded in solving her housing problem.
I think it is agreed by all that any stimulus to the building industry has an immediate effect upon other industries. I submit that the findings of the public bodies to which I have referred, and the various reports which have been published, make it abundantly clear that the situation in Canada with regard to housing is grave. The Montreal Metropolitan commission undertook a survey which was carried out in a very painstaking manner, and I think the report they made is more than fair. They do not attempt to exaggerate the situation in any way. A total of 4,216 houses were inspected and the following conclusions reached:
According to the Central Housing Committee, Washington, D.C., in a recently published glossary of housing terms, a slum is defined as "an area in which dwellings predominate that because of either dilapidation, obsolescence, overcrowding, arrangement or design, lack of ventilation, light or sanitary facilities, or a combination of these factors are detrimental to the safety, health, morals, comfort and welfare of the inhabitants thereof."
If we accept the above definition, we are bound to affirm that there are districts in Montreal which can aptly be described as " slum areas."
They probably do not dramatically reflect each and every one of the characteristics mentioned in the foregoing definition. Overcrowding is not in wide evidence. Sanitary facilities are, on the whole, passable. But these districts do embrace predominantly old housing. Much of it is obsolescent, a considerable portion of it is dilapidated. The arrangement or design of the dwellings, either in their structural defects or the manner in which they are crowded on the land, along with "a combination of other factors are detrimental to the safety, health, morals, comfort and welfare of the inhabitants thereof."
In this sense Montreal has a slum problem.
The report continues:
As such, they represent an economic liability, the social costs of which are too expensive a luxury for us to indefinitely continue to tolerate.
Passing across the country, we find the following statement made by Dr. T. A. Lomer of Ottawa:
The scarcity of reasonably low rental houses is so great that the health department has not been able to take action to abate overcrowding except in the most extreme cases.
The chief inspector of the health department at Winnipeg has this to say:
From time to time this department has drawn attention to the increasing congestion by the conversion of one-family dwellings into tenements or multiple dwellings; housing from two to ten families. Nothing was being done to such houses to make them fit for multiple occupation, except that in order to attract tenants, gas stoves were installed in the various rooms. Pages have been written about the undesirable conditions thus being created; the lack of adequate plumbing, want of ventilation, occupation of cellars and attics, danger from fire, danger from communicable disease propagation, increased expense to the city for hospitalization, the moral effects of such conditions, etc.
And again:
-during the past five years, only one house or suite has been provided for every ten marriages.
An authority in Saskatchewan has this to say:
Saskatchewan has the doubtful honour of being the most overcrowded province, from the point of view of housing, in the entire dominion.
The report of a special committee appointed by the city council of Vancouver to investigate housing conditions contains the following paragraph:
Apart from overcrowding, a very unfortunate condition is being perpetuated in connection with dilapidated, and in some cases, condemned dwellings. Under ordinary circumstances, these buildings would stand vacant, or be demolished, but the great lack of suitable accommodation has forced people to occupy these premises to the detriment of their health and well being. The rentals obtained are small and, therefore, the landlords will carry out no repairs, nor make any improvements; thus, damp and cold add their toll to the misery of the occupants.
This report is signed by Helena R. Gutte-ridge, chairman of the building, civic planning and parks committee. The Vancouver branch of the National Planning and Housing Association has this to say:
There is at present an acute shortage of housing accommodation in Vancouver. Apartment house surveys reveal that less than one per cent of the suites are vacant, and the position with regard to the cheapest types of accommodation is worse still. It is practically impossible to find a vacant house in the poorer districts.
The housing shortage not only results in overcrowding; it also prevents the effective
The Address-Mr. MacNeil

enforcement of the sanitary and zoning by-laws, since it becomes impossible to remove tenants from insanitary dwellings. The reports of the medical health officer indicate that there are many buildings occupied as dwellings which would not ordinarily pass for that purpose.
A recent civic housing survey revealed serious overcrowding and slum conditions in many rooming houses. It also disclosed that over 600 persons (including children) are living in shacks or houseboats on the waterfront, all without sewage facilities and mostly without a direct water supply. Unless active measures of prevention arc immediately undertaken, these conditions will continue to spread and multiply.
The population of Vancouver has increased by over 12.000 during the last two years. New houses built during this period provided accommodation for less than half this increase in population, and were mainly of a type far beyond the means of the lower paid sections of the community. Marriages deferred from the depression, the "unscrambling" of families, and the steady decline in the size of the family unit, has still further aggravated the situation.
They give the number of houses and apartments which have been built in Vancouver during the last six years. The report continues:
It is estimated that an annual output of at least 2,000 houses a year for the next six yea-rs is required to make good the existing shortage.
At the date of the 1931 census, nearly 40 per cent of the families renting houses in Vancouver were paying under $25 a month in rent, and their average income was approximately $70 per month. Allowing one-fifth of income for rent, the average rent which this group can afford to pay is under $15 a month. About half of the population own (or have an equity in) their own homes. The other half, and probably a good proportion of those who have attempted to buy their homes, have, for the most part, neither the capital nor the stability of income to justify house purchase.
Unassisted private enterprise cannot build satisfactory houses to rent at under $30 per month.
The 1935 Housing Act does not touch the problem of the lower paid worker, since the average cost of the 154 houses (including land) so far built in British Columbia under the act, is over $4,400. Direct governmental assistance for low cost housing is therefore essential.
8. The key to the situation is cheap finance, since financing charges usually represent well over half the net rent. The dominion is alone in a position to provide this financial assistance, and without it the municipalities are powerless to act.
He goes on to point out:
Public responsibility for housing conditions has been accepted in Europe for many years.
I think it has been made abundantly clear that the situation is grave and demands action by this parliament, and I urge that such action be taken soon. When we review housing conditions across Canada, I think we will agree with the statement made by

Professor Percy E. Nobbs, in a report of a recent survey of the situation in Montreal in conjunction with the junior board of trade:
Private enterprise has never been able to cope with the problem of providing decent accommodation at these rentals for low-wage families. Large-scale operations and corporate management combined with a measure of social service are the only solution . . . Bad housing is often profitable to the landlords, but never to the community; for it carries with it vast economic burdens, many of which are calculable to a fraction of a cent-hospitalization, juvenile delinquency, etc. It is on purely economic grounds that I urge rehabilitation loans to retard the growth of slums, and large scale housing operations, as a prelude to slum clearance later on. The alternative is to see society destroyed by the mounting burdens due to bad environment.
I submit that in view of these conditions so well described, it would be not only sound economy but wise statesmanship to introduce without delay a measure to extend the housing program to provide low rental and low cost houses.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, some of the measures to be submitted to parliament during this session deserve the very serious attention of the legislator. Trade agreements, constitutional amendments, unemployment insurance, assistance to agriculture, the economic situation of the country, constitutionality of legislation, repression of agitators, and all that is required for the sound administration of the state. As to trade agreements, not only do they contribute largely to Canada's economic recovery, but they help to establish peaceful relations between nations. Were those their only advantages they would deserve the most careful attention of the people's representatives and our whole-hearted support in so far as they tend to benefit our people.
In this troubled world the efforts of our rulers should tend solely towards peace, the creator of initiative, of work and of happiness, but nothing is more difficult to-day than to unite the best elements of the country for the attainment of that ideal. The endeavours of statesmen to give to the country the best possible administration are constantly beset by the most serious obstacles. However, in spite of adverse winds, the ship is making for the port where prosperity so long in sight, awaits its arrival.
Let us not forget, sir, that it is by farming that we have lived as a colony and that we shall survive as a nation. That is true not only of Quebec but of all the provinces of Canada. To the great agricultural industry I am resolved to bring, as in the past, all my help and the experience I have acquired

The Address-Mr. Lacombe
in this chamber. As to the matter of unemployment insurance, it should in my humble opinion be approached with the greatest care and considered only to the extent that it will put an end to the depressing and disastrous method of direct relief. I go further: better have no unemployment insurance than allow provincial prerogatives to suffer.
During the past week there has been the question of submitting certain provincial laws to the consideration of the supreme court. One of these laws is known as the "Padlock Act" passed by the Quebec Legislature. At all events, should the highest court of the country hold this law unconstitutional, it would be the federal government's own duty to take immediate measures to curb agitators, by whatever name they call themselves. All revolutionary movements and organizations should be promptly, firmly, energetically and effectively suppressed by the government. For do they not constitute an attack upon established authority? Do they not provoke deep reactions among the masses, thus preparing the decline of the authority of the state and the constitution of the country?
Nobody will deny that for some time there has been a marked improvement in more than one sphere. The number of relief recipients was reduced. Better prices prevailed for certain kinds of farm products. However there is still room for improvement from a social and economic viewpoint. Small wage earners and farmers wrere the most severely affected by the economic unrest which prevailed during these last few years. Our young people were in great distress. The governments made commendable efforts to remedy these deplorable conditions. However, we need something besides theories, speeches, and lectures, in order to reestablish the condition of all classes in our community. From the people we require initiative and enterprise; from the governments, efficiency in their administration, and a clear vision of present requirements. Thus, the present government, who enjoy the confidence of the people, may carry on their work or reconstruction, in the interest of the country and its ratepayers.
Since the speech from the throne allows the members to make all the suggestions which they consider as being in the public interest, I shall draw the attention of the government to the small salaries which are being paid to our rural carriers for the carrying of his majesty's mail, in certain parts of the country. Some may contend that these carriers have freely agreed to the salary they are getting. It is true that contracts are let out only after a call for tenders. It is also true
that, except for some serious reasons, the contract is awarded to the lowest bidder. Is that a good reason to deprive these carriers of the reward of their labour? I know some pitiful cases where carriers have been operating at a loss for two years.
Mr. Speaker, on all sides you hear of nothing but social justice, minimum wages, and fair remuneration of labour. Still, rural carriers, who shoulder great responsibilities, are most unfairly treated, when you consider the expenses they incur to carry out their work for his majesty. I regret very much to be precluded by the rules of this house from introducing a bill in order to grant these rural mail carriers a reasonable salary and a fair remuneration. In fact, only a minister of the crown may introduce such a bill. That is why, for the sake of fairness, and justice, I would ask the hon. Postmaster General (Mr. Elliott) to submit to parliament the necessary measure, since I have not the right to do so myself. Otherwise, the government will give the people the edifying spectacle of men being exploited while carrying his majesty's mail. I shall probably be told in reply to my request that the Post Office Department and the carriers are already bound by a contract. An empty excuse! When any legislation in force constitutes a denial of justice toward the people of a country, the first duty of the government is to amend it or to substitute another therefor. Besides, it would be easy, in the notice calling for tenders, to fix a minimum annual rate of, say, $35 per mile provided of course, the government were satisfied that the tender system was the best one. Moreover, in the notice and request for tenders it should be clearly and definitely stated that any tender involving a rate of compensation lower, for example, than the annual rate of $35 per mile, shall be deemed null and void.
Mr. Speaker, I should have liked to discuss other problems of national importance, such as the defence estimates. But "all in good time," as the saying goes. Therefore, when the National Defence department's estimates are brought up in the house I shall, as I have done before, consider and discuss them in such a manner and spirit as appear to me in the best interests of Canada. When that troublesome question comes up, I shall be governed by no other consideration than the love of my country and its welfare and progress.
In concluding, I wish to tell the house that I shall, again this year, insist upon the application of a seasonal tariff for the benefit of
The Address-Mr. Hansell

truck gardeners in my constituency and in the whole country. When, at the very first session of this parliament, the government gave favourable consideration to my resolution requesting a seasonal tariff for fruit and vegetable producers, an immediate improvement was noticed in the selling price of these nationally important products. Truck gardening holds a prominent place in the economic life of Canada. Therefore, not only should the government help that industry to preserve its present standing, but it should also promote its development in the best interests of the Canadian people.

Mr. Speaker, a member sitting in this corner and being from Alberta can hardly rise in this house to-day without adverting to the now famous Powell and Unwin case recently concluded. The press has had a	good deal to say during past
months concerning this matter, and in yesterday's newspapers we read of the telegram that had been sent the right hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) from the Attorney General of Alberta requesting the full remission of these sentences. To-day's press carries the news that the Minister of Justice has not seen his way clear to granting the request. The charge against these gentlemen would appear to be, and is generally accepted to be, actuated by political motivation. This being the case, one might be excused for having entertained the hope that the Minister of Justice would see his way clear to grant the dignified request of His Majesty's Attorney General for the Province of Alberta, especially when it is borne in mind that Alberta's attorney general, being on the ground and therefore intimately familiar with all aspects of the situation involved, is singularly qualified to make recommendations as to the disposition of the sentences. The Minister of Justice having made his decision, I feel impelled to ask that he sympathetically consider the possibility of granting at a very early date a parole for these persecuted gentlemen, who are after all the servants of the people of Alberta.
I had not intended to speak to the motion for an address in reply to the speech from the throne, but after listening to several remarks that have been made in debate thus far I am compelled to say a few words on some matters. I wish to refer particularly to certain remarks made by the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Mclvor) wherein he endeavours to justify the argument against the present policy of subventions on coal. The hon. gentleman made considerable reference to this matter

during the last session, and I think that he should be better informed. It is generally argued by those living at the head of the lakes that subventions on coal destroy to a very large extent the shipping industry at the head of the great lakes. It is argued by some that millions of dollars have been invested in elevators, coal docks and harbour improvements on the assumption that the natural advantage of the harbours at Fort William and Port Arthur as shipping centres assures their future growth and improvement. But those who so argue overlook the fact that millions of dollars have been invested in the coal industry of Alberta upon the assumption that the people of Canada need coal and should naturally buy home products.
In an editorial that appeared in the Daily Times-Journal of Fort William about a year ago the statement was made that the destruction of the coal trade at the head of the lakes was the result of deliberate action on the part of the government in response to agitation for subventions on the part of western coal operators. It is stated that because of the subvention policy the amount of coal handled at the head of the lakes dropped about one and a quarter million tons. In reply let me say that the policy of subventions for coal was instituted by a Liberal government, first in Nova Scotia and later in the west. The fact that subventions were granted to Nova Scotia gave the coal mining industry in the west a natural right to expect that the same thing would be done for it. The statement that this coal subvention policy reduced the coal trade at the head of the lakes one and a quarter million tons is entirely incorrect. The movement of Alberta and British Columbia coal under the subvention has never exceeded
340.000	tons, and part of this goes to points in eastern Ontario which were never served from Fort William. The hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Mclvor) seems very much concerned about the employment of 100 to 150 men in his constituency. The movement of
340.000	tons of coal from the west gives employment to something like 400 miners and partial employment to some 2,250 trainmen, in addition to other railroad employees who otherwise would be put on short time or thrown entirely on relief. In addition there are farmers in western Canada who are able to make ends meet by selling mine props made from timber cut from their small forests. The editorial referred to would lead the public to believe that Alberta coal is of inferior quality to imported coals. The very opposite is the fact. That is proved by actual tests.

The Address-Mr. Hansell
We have coals in Alberta and in Nova Scotia that compare most favourably with any imported coal.
It is also suggested that by doing away with coal subventions and importing additional coal from the United States the amount of the subvention would be saved and the revenue increased by the duty collected. Such an argument is untenable, for if it were carried to its logical conclusion we would be, in effect, saying: Destroy all Canadian industry and reap the revenue collected in duty on imports. But money spent on our own coal production at least stays in the country, and that part paid to employees and railway men, as well as any small dividends or profits to the operators, also remains in Canada, except perhaps a small amount. Most important of all is that if the comparatively small amount now being spent for western subventions, about $300,000, were discontinued and such coal displaced by United States coal, the result would be more unemployment, more relief costs, and money going abroad, thus reducing the purchasing power of the Canadian people and placing upon them a greater burden of taxation.
The hon. member said, as reported on page 104 of Hansard:
I do not like to see western coal coming down to within a few miles of Fort William to the detriment of our workers.
Surely my hon. friend does not mean that he desires the destruction of an entire coal mining industry with its thousands of employees in order to employ 100 to 150 men in his constituency. He must remember that to interfere with subventions in western Canada would mean that there would have to be the same interference with subventions for Nova Scotia coal, thus destroying the entire coal mining industry of Canada. I believe the coal mining industry of Canada is a matter of national importance, and we are dealing with national policies. What should be done to save the coal mining industry of this country, under the present system at least, is to increase the subvention.
The hon. member said also that he viewed with alarm any action taken by any province to curtail the freedom of the press. I have discussed this matter with some of my colleagues. I know it is contrary to parliamentary procedure to discus a matter which is before the courts, but I find nothing in the rules to prevent me from simply reading the act which was passed by the Alberta legislature. I would like to have your ruling on this Mr. Speaker...

speechtext:
I shall read it without any comment whatsoever. 'It is Bill No. 9, entitled, "An Act to Ensure the Publication of Accurate News and Information," and it reads:
Whereas it is expedient and in the public interest that the newspapers published in the province should furnish to the people of the province statements made by the authority of the government of the province as to the true and exact objects of the policy of the government and as to the hindrances to or difficulties in achieving such objects, to the end that the people may be informed with respect thereto.
Now therefore His Majesty, by and with the advice and consent of the legislative assembly of the province of Alberta enacts as follows:
1.	This act may be cited as "The Accurate News and Information Act."
2.	In this act, unless the context otherwise requiresfa) "Chairman" means the chairman of the board constituted by section 3 of the Alberta Social Credit Act;
(b) "Newspaper" means a paper containing public news, intelligence or occurrences or remarks or observations thereon, printed for sale and published periodically in parts or numbers at regular intervals not exceeding thirty-one days between the publication of any two of such papers, parts or numbers, and includes a paper printed in order to be made public w-eekly or oftener, or at intervals not exceeding thirty-one days containing only or principally advertisements, and a paper containing accounts of events occurring within thirty-one days before the date of publication.
3.	(1) Subject to the other provisions of this section, every person who is the proprietor, editor, publisher or manager of any newspaper published in the province, shall when required so to do by the chairman, publish in that newspaper any statement furnished by the chairman which has for its object the correction or amplification of any statement relating to any policy or activity of the government of the province published by that newspaper within the next preceding thirty-one days.
(2)	Every such statement shall have written upon it a certificate in the following words: "The foregoing statement is published by the direction of the chairman of the social credit board," which certificate shall be printed at the foot of the statement to which it relates.
(3)	Every such statement shall be printed with the type ordinarily used in the printing of the newspaper.
(4)	The length of any statement required to be published shall not exceed the length of the statement corrected thereby and such statement shall be given the same prominence as to position, type and space as the statement corrected thereby.
(5)	Every requirement by the chairman for the publication of any statement shall be in writing signed by the chairman, and shall be deemed to have been duly made upon the receipt of the requirement together with the statements referred to therein at the office or usual place of business of any of the following persons, namely, the proprietor, editor, publisher or manager of the newspaper.
The Address-Mr. Hansell

(6)	Every statement so required to be published in a newspaper shall be submitted in the language used in the publication of such newspaper .and shall be published in the next regular issue thereof after the day upon which the requirement for the publication thereof referred to in subsection (5) is received at the office or usual place of business of any of the following persons, namely, the proprietor, editor, publisher or manager of the newspaper.
(7)	No statement required to be published pursuant to this act shall contain any notice or other matter the publication of which is required to be made pursuant to any other statute or which is ordinarily published as advertising.
4.	Every person who is the proprietor, editor, publisher or manager of any newspaper, shall upon being required so to do by the chairman in writing, within twenty-four hours after the delivery of such requirement at the office or usual place of business of any of the following persons, namely, the proprietor, editor, publisher or manager of the newspaper, make a return in writing setting out every source from which any information emanated, as to any statement contained in any issue of the newspaper published within sixty days of the making of the requirement and the names, addresses and occupations of all persons by whom such information was furnished to the newspaper, and the name and address of the writer of any editorial, article or news item contained in any such issue of the newspaper as aforesaid.
5.	No action for libel shall be maintainable on account of the publication of any statement pursuant to this act against any person who is the proprietor, editor, publisher, manager or printer of the new'spaper publishing the same or against any employee of any such person or against any person on account of any subsequent publication of any such statement.
6.	In case the proprietor, editor, publisher or manager of any newspaper has been guilty of any contravention of any of the provisions of this act the lieutenant governor in council, upon the recommendation of the chairman, may by order prohibit,-
(a)	the publication of such newspaper either for a definite time or until further order;
(b)	the publication in any newspaper of anything written by any person specified in the order;
(c)	the publication of any information emanating from any person or source specified in the order.
7.	(1) Every person who contravenes any of the provisions of this act or who makes any default in complying with any requirement made in pursuance of this act shall be liable to a penalty not to exceed five hundred dollars.
(2)	Every person who contravenes any of the provisions of any order in council made pursuant to section 6 of this act shall in respect of every such contravention be liable to a penalty not to exceed one thousand dollars.
(3)	Any penalty which any person is liable to pay pursuant to any provision of this act shall be recoverable either by suit brought by the chairman in any court of competent civil jurisdiction, or upon summary conviction upon

the information or complaint of the chairman or of some person authorized in writing by the chairman to lay such information.
8.	This act shall come into force on the day upon which it is assented to.
Now my hon. friend can read the act for his own information. I am not going to make any comment on it whatever, but I wish to deal with one phase of thought that is prevalent in the minds of many people, relative to what is meant by the freedom of the press. It seems to me the freedom of the press means that it is free to print the truth. Let us make no mistake about that; it is free to print the truth. The hon. member for Fort William, who made this reference,. is a clergyman. Perhaps it is only fitting that one clergyman should reply to another.
