I have only ten minutes
in which to finish my observations, and I should like to spend the time in answering the hon. member for North Huron. He has been viewing the Alberta situation from a distance. May I now bring information from Alberta showing what some Liberals in that province think of the battle which was supposed to be fought in this house against the money powers. Before proceeding to the reference, may I ask when the battle was fought. If it has been fought, when was it finished? If it is finished, who won the victory? If it is finished, was the victory won by parliament or by the money powers? If it is not finished, why was money reform absent from the speech from the throne?
I have said that I would let the hon. member view the matter from the standpoint of people who are a little nearer the situation. All hon. members have received a letter from the Legislative Assembly of Manitoba. That assembly is substantially Liberal, and yet we find that it does not recognize that a battle has been fought or won. This is the resolution moved and carried by the legislature of Manitoba:
Whereas the standard of living in Canada can only be raised by increased production and consumption of goods and services,
Whereas such increased production and consumption can only be accomplished effectively by national control of currency and credit issued in terms of public need,
Whereas the government of Canada, by recent legislation, now control fifty-one per cent of the shares of the Bank of Canada,
Now, therefore, be it resolved that in the opinion of this legislature that the government of Canada proceed forthwith to implement its election pledges and issue through the Bank of Canada currency and credit, considered in terms of public need, the amount of which to be determined in relation to the domestic and industrial requirements of the Canadian people.
Be it further resolved that a copy of this resolution be sent to the premier of Canada, every member of his cabinet, and all members of the House of Commons.
That, Mr. Speaker, comes from the legislature of Manitoba.

In the -five minutes left at my disposal may I deal with what some people from Alberta who are interested in Liberal policies have to say. In that connection I shall read a letter from a gentleman who during the last election campaign was an organizer for the Liberal forces in Alberta. This letter was written to the Prime Minister and, so far as I can learn, has not yet been acknowledged. In sending a copy of the letter to the Edmonton Bulletin the gentleman in question wrote:
Editor
Bulletin.
On August 10th the writer sent the enclosed letter to Right Honourable W. L. Mackenzie King, Premier of Canada.
Having supported his government in the 1933 election in reliance upon his election pledges, the courtesy of an acknowledgment was deemed reasonable whether the explanation was satisfactory or not.
The people should know how those of us who worked and voted for his election, now feel about the present situation.
This is the letter:
Right Honourable W. L. Mackenzie King, Prime Minister,
Ottawa, Canada.
Dear Mr. King:
Edmonton's recent unique legislative activities must have shocked Ottawa nearly as much as Ottawa's continued inactivity on the same question has disappointed and disheartened the west.
Alberta's misguided and desperate attempts to secure for her citizens as a life-sustaining necessity, an increase in her people's purchasing power in view of Ottawa's failure therein, has resulted in the present legislation.
The writer opposed the social credit idea of monthly "dividends" not because relief from the present situation was not required, but because that group was proposing to grant purchasing power in a way that seemed beyond the province's constitutional powers to accomplish, whereas you, on behalf of the Liberal party of Canada, to which I belong because I believe in a minimum of tariff barriers to trade, and which I helped as local organizer at election time, had given a definite pledge on behalf of the Liberals of Canada, to remedy the long standing financial and economic injustice to the Canadian people due to the shackles imposed upon commercial and economic progress by the Bank Act which farms out the national credit to private interests for their profit rather than for the nation's welfare.
Your pledge, given in parliament in 1934 and which formed the chief plank in the Liberal platform when they were returned to power under your leadership is widely known and well remembered. It is as follows:
" Once a nation parts with the control of its currency and credit it matters not who makes the nation's laws. Usury, once in control, will wreck any nation. Until the control of the issue of currency and credit is restored to the government and recognized as its most conspicuous and sacred responsibility, all talk of

The Address-Mr. Hansell
sovereignty of parliament and of democracy is idle and futile. ... To regain for the nation what has thus been lost will continue to be the first objective of Liberal effort."
That pledge is incorporated in the speech from the throne reported on page 17 of the 1936 Hansard, after your government took office, in the following words:
" The control of credit, and the issue of currency, being public matters of direct concern to every citizen, it is intended, at the present session, to ask parliament to make such changes in the ownership and control of the Bank of Canada, as may be necessary to give to the government a predominant interest in the ownership as well as effective control of the bank."
In the 1936 session of parliament you mentioned for example the development of the tourist trade as a proper and desirable activity of the National Employment Commission. Mr. Bennett agreed, and there was general parliamentary and other agreement on the subject.
That meant highway construction-of necessity involved the spending of money.
What has happened in that regard?
Alberta has the finest scenery in the world but it can't be observed because of bad roads.
In this connection it will be noted that the changes you requested in the set-up of the Bank of Canada were made which enabled your government to control the country's credit and to issue the necessary currency to accomplish on a wide front the building and improving of national highways.
Why did you want the government to have power of control over credit and the issue of currency if that power was not going to be exercised for the people's benefit?
The 1936 session of parliament produced a number of earnest voices insistent that such power be restored to the government and used.
What happened to those voices?
Why were Tucker, and McGeer, and Stitt, and others who last year were insistent upon the people's rights being exercised, silent in the 1937 session? What assurance did you give that induced them to remain silent in the face of an ever growing necessity for action?
The people are asking this and they insist on knowing.
As you are recognized personally as an outstanding authority on economics, your election pledge had more weight than that of a person not so equipped. As you had an unimpeachable private record your word was accepted.
The only suggested explanation of your inertia since then, in the face of a condition of increasing need, would appear to be lack of courage.
Is that the trouble? Or do you now doubt your estimate of existing conditions, and the correctness of your remedy? Or, again, is it your purpose to make the Bank of Canada a useful adjunct to the chartered banking system (to repeat the words of the general manager of the Royal Bank of Canada in his address to the bank shareholders at their annual meeting in January, 1934)?
If you were correct, as we still confidently believe, when are you going to do something about it? You can't wait forever, because people's lives and their living-their hopes for the future are at stake. Old people, too old to get work if it could be had, and too young to get the meagre old age pension- are sick with defeat. Middle aged people, if employed, find their tenure of employment less and less secure, and their remuneration diminishing while living costs rise. If they are unemployed, their spirits are utterly broken by the sense of helplessness and, worse still, of uselessness which grips them. Young people cannot make plans for their life work or for marriage or homes or families of their own, and the spark of ambition is quenched.
Desperate people are apt to take desperate measures and go to any extreme to maintain their God given right to live. And where only the outworn, criminally conceived system, which your government has both the power and a specific mandate from the people to replace, stands in the way of this right, how can they be prevented or blamed for doing so, if you continue to refuse to act?
The time for effective, constructive, intelligent action is overdue.
What are you going to do about it?
The hopes and the prayers of a stricken people are yours as you let your conscience direct your intelligence to effective action in this crisis.
Awaiting your explanation and reply, I am, sir, on behalf of myself and all western Canadians.
Yours sincerely,
A. L. Marks.
Mr. Marks is a well known lawyer and a respected citizen of Edmonton. I hope the hon. member for North Huron (Mr. Deach-man) and the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) will take notice of these things. To repeat what the hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Mitchell) said yesterday, Alberta is not playing a game; she is tackling a problem which the Prime Minister of this country promised the country he himself would tackle. With these remarks I ask the house to take notice that we in this corner are insisting upon a solution of the problem which confronts Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I represent a riding, that of Athabaska, which is in the area known as the park land section of Alberta. Into that area during the last five or six years have come farmers from the dust bowl of the west, men who have been defeated in their efforts to make a living there, and are now pioneering in Alberta under conditions very closely approximating those which our ancestors had to face in Ontario a hundred years ago. They have come into that area without their implements, or with just the remnants of them, and such stock, as they were able to save from the wreck. This summer, when I was there, I found them heroically facing conditions which, had I the time to tell hon. members here about, I am sure would deepen their feelings of sympathy and respect for the courage and fortitude of these people who, having seen the things they gave their lives to, broken, are stooping to build them up again with worn-out tools.
One question which the people on the farnu are asking-and it is a question that I have always asked myself, born and reared as I was on a farm in Ontario-is, Why are the farmers unable to have the same incomes as the people in the cities? It seems a selfevident truth that the farmers, who are literally feeding and clothing the world, should be entitled, from the standpoint of the social value of the services they render, to remuneration comparable with that received by those who manufacture wool and hides into clothing and shoes, or lumber into chairs and furniture, or those who render services to society professionally. That is a question to which I hope we can begin to find an answer before parliament prorogues.
During the last two weeks members of the house from different parts of Canada have told us about conditions in their various ridings, and I was particularly	interested in	thespeeches made by the hon. member for Huron North (Mr. Deachman) and the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Hyndman). I want to congratulate the hon. member for Huron North on the effectual analysis of operating costs which he presented to the house showing the income and expenditures of the farmers of Ontario, analyzing their investments and	showing	their	net income, fromwhich the	startling	fact	emerged that	thefarmers of	Ontario	are	receiving less	remuneration than the wages of a junio'r office boy. less than one dollar a day, he said. The 
hon. member for Carleton said that seventy-five per cent of the farms in Ontario were mortgaged. Well, Mr. Speaker, I can say that in the new sections of Athabaska, in the park areas where settlement is taking place under pioneering conditions, the farmers have neither investments nor electric lights. The hon. member for Huron North spoke about the cost of electricity to the farmer, and I just want to say that the farmers in my district have neither electricity nor investments.
The reason I refer to the addresses made by these two gentlemen is that they are members of parties which have alternated in power, administering the affairs of this country for the last seventy years since confederation, and looking at the situation from the standpoint from which any institution or policy or system must be judged, by the fruits it produces, the net results are those pathetic and heart-breaking conditions which have been described by these two hon. members.
I do not know whether other hon. members have noticed it or not, but since coming to Ottawa this session I have been impressed by the fact that among members of all parties- and I have had the pleasure and privilege of talking with members of all parties in the house-I have found a serious undertone, a grave, earnest desire to make a contribution to the solution of the perplexing problems that confront us. As I met these men and talked in a heart to heart fashion with them, my feeling of comradeship and respect has been deepened. It is true they are here to represent different political and economic philosophies; but it seems to me that there is a growing tendency towards the recognition of the fact that we have all failed, and that our common task is to find a way to lay the foundations of a plan that will endure. Indeed, that kindliness and magnanimity, and the evident desire to be friendly, is a characteristic of all the people that I meet, when I meet them man to man.
During the last twenty-five years of my life I have lived and rubbed shoulders in western Canada with people from every land beneath the sun. I have in my riding representatives of most of the races that have come from the older parts of the world, and I find in them the same kindliness. I venture to say that no one of these peoples desires to injure his fellow man in other countries. It makes me think of the words of the great French philosopher. Rousseau, who said, about two hundred years ago, "Men are naturally good. It is by their institutions alone that they become corrupt." If men are naturally

The Address-Mr. Rowe (Athabaska)
good and have a desire to cooperate with each other, surely we can recognize the equal worth of all peoples and races, the common blood and common destiny of mankind, and try in our policies to remember that the world is interdependent culturally, economically, and spiritually, if you will; that we are just beginning to get acquainted; and that we should not do or say anything, or institute any policy which would injure or invade the rights of people in other countries.
I can never forgive Herbert Spencer for having written that manifesto, on which I believe the constitution of Japan was founded, in which he said that society flourishes by the antagonism of its atoms. I believe on the contrary that the obvious golden truth is that constructive cooperation and not destructive combativeness is the rule by which we must be guided, because the former is the first principle of life upon which the universe is founded, the principle of self-preservation by which we seek to avoid friction. That is true of every atom in life and of every individual in society. We must seek the minimum of frustration and the avoidance of friction.
Just the other day there came to my desk a cartoon called Two Mules, a fable for the Nations. In the first cartoon two mules are pictured tied together with a rope. There are two stacks of hay, one on each side of the mules which are tethered in such a way that by going together they can reach either stack. They are looking at the hay in pleasurable anticipation. In the second picture each is straining to reach the stack nearest him and pulling against the other. In the third picture they are kicking, each refusing to go with the other. All they lack is understanding; they do not know how to cooperate. In the fourth picture they have decided to sit down and talk it over, and there is a large interrogation mark between them. The hay is still there. In the fifth picture they decide to cooperate constructively and they are consuming the hay. They are both standing by one of the stacks. In the last picture they are eating the other stack.
I am not going to suggest that we should have horse sense; perhaps that is too much to expect of the human family; but I do suggest that we have at least mule sense.
Five hundred years ago the Indians ruled this country and the standard of living they enjoyed was measured by their collective capacity to produce wealth. The very young children and the very old men and women lived off the surplus that could be produced by those who caught fish in the lakes and
rivers and game in the forest. The one yardstick by which the Indians measured their standard of living was their collective capacity to produce wealth. If there was a bad year, then, of course, they were short; perhaps there was famine; but in a good year everybody was happy.
I want to draw a little picture of what would have happened among the Indians had their wise counsellors and leaders, their medicine men, if you like, informed them that a policy of "scarcity" had been decided upon and that a certain percentage of the strong young men should go back into the stockade, sit down and twiddle their thumbs, notwithstanding the fact that the rivers and lakes were teeming with fish and the woods were filled with game. Another percentage of young men, let us say, were asked to go into the northern part of the country and dig a curious yellow metal out of the ground, transport it laboriously to the mouth of the Hudson river and bury it in another hole in the ground. Because that metal could not be eaten, because it could not be worn or burned to warm them in their wigwams, the labour that these men performed in the production and transport of gold was all wasted. It was not wealth at all, and those who toiled in the forest and on the rivers and lakes to produce game and fish had to support these men who had dug up this gold. Then it was decided that a certain percentage should engage in the production of goods for shipment abroad; there was to be foreign trade. So that notwithstanding the fact that these goods were needed at home these men had to go to work and produce a certain quantity of goods to be shipped out of the country. Then, because it was necessary for some of the men to leave the country sometimes to fight for the right to continue sending abroad goods that were needed at home, a certain percentage of braves had to undergo training in order to engage in death duels with members of other tribes. And they, too, had to be fed and clothed.
I wonder how long it would have taken those young braves to discover that their witch-doctors and medicine-men were nothing but imbeciles to be locked up or put out of the way as painlessly as possible. Yet that is an accurate picture of what is going on in Canada to-day. Last year the nations of the world produced and distributed, by borrowing, fifteen billions worth of armaments and munitions. Every dollar of that was wasted; every dollar of it came out of useful labour. If the people in other countries bought from us metals which were used in the manufacture of war materials their governments had to tax

The Address-Mr. Rowe (Athabaska)
them to pay for these commodities, and therefore their standard of living was reduced exactly by the cost of these implements of war. I do not think there can be any answer to that.
I have observed a few things which I wish to call to the attention of hon. members with respect to foreign affairs and our foreign policy. In the first place I wish to commend warmly the action of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) in going to Berlin last year. I covet for Canada leadership in the direction of instituting measures which will reduce the cause of the friction, fear, animosity and antagonism which exist between ourselves and that great nation, a nation that has established itself as one of the foremost among the peoples of the world in science and art and culture. Anything that can be done to break down prejudices, to assure these people that we do not desire their harm, is all to the good. But I wonder whether the Prime Minister did not make a slip in Paris, because there seems to be a conflict between his views and those of the hon. member (Mr. Francoeur) who moved the address in reply to the speech from the throne. He said that we do not intend to engage in foreign wars; that we do not intend anything but defence. Yet the Prime Minister said that if Britain finds herself in trouble she will find Canada at her side. There seems to be a contradiction there. I call attention to the fact that those interests which we might be called upon to defend in some foreign country were the result of a defect in the present economic system in its development one hundred years ago. The workers who produced that wealth were not paid enough to enable them to buy back the goods, and therefore there came about the rise of capital investments by Great Britain in other countries. These capital investments have proved a boomerang, because when they were used to develop industries abroad Britain found herself in competition with other countries as a result of the export of her surplus. I want it clearly understood as far as I am concerned that if patriotism means the art of inducing someone who has no interests at home to defend someone else's interests abroad, then we had better revise our idea of patriotism. I suggest further that it takes neither moral nor physical courage to arrange wars for other people to fight. Most hon. members are beyond the age to be conscripted, but I suggest that we should be very careful about the policies we institute, policies of foreign trade which give rise to conflict resulting in war. It is very easy to 
launch such policies, but it would be a different thing if we were made to go out and fight for policies that we initiated.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) in his broadcast on September 19, said:
Canada is anxious and prepared to do whatever lies within her power to promote the widest measure of international cooperation.
I read in the Canadian Press dispatch from New York of February 4:
Canada prepares for her display at New York fair.
Plans for Canadian participation in the New York World's Fair next year moved ahead to-day as fair officials announced the dominion had contracted for 40,000 square feet of space and would send destroyers and airplanes as a ceremonial gesture.
That is a peculiar kind of "ceremonial gesture".
Then there is the question of our policy of defence. The statement of the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Mackenzie), in initiating what he calls an " adequate policy " of defence, that it is necessary to keep down subversive elements from within, has been repeated many times in the house. The Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) said repeatedly last year and again this year that the way to control subversive elements is to remove the cause. That is a sound principle. I mention that to show members of the government that there appears to be something there which requires explanation. I believe that most if not all of the so-called moral diseases of mankind are due to the abnormal conditions under which people have been compelled to live. If that is true, obviously the cure consists in nothing less than removing the cause. And the cause is to be found in the conflict arising out of competition, competition that is unnecessary. We have to ask ourselves whether if we were to utilize the productive capacity of our machinery in the factories and the farms of this country with a view to producing goods and services to be consumed by our people, it is possible to produce enough for all. I think it is. Therefore I suggest that a system based upon competition has now become outworn and is an anachronism. It is necessary now to undertake some mental readjustment to keep pace with the changing needs of society. I would also call attention to the rather optimistic suggestion in the speech from the throne to the effect that conditions in Canada are fairly good, and suggest that it is a mistake to measure them by comparison with what has happened in the past or what is happening in other countries. The only accurate measure of value when we are

The Address-Mr. Rowe (Athabaska)
evaluating the soundness of our policies is, what is it possible to do with the machinery we have?
I should like to congratulate the Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. Crerar) on the broadcasts which he has made throughout Canada about our natural resources. Of course it is commonly understood that education is vested in the provinces; but this form of education is in my opinion invaluable, in creating an informed, enlightened, intelligent public opinion by disseminating factual and scientific information about Canada and what we possess. But I should like to suggest that our great mineral wealth is badly needed to provide the comforts of life for our own people. I should like to see our mineral wealth diverted from channels of destruction into channels of construction. I should like to think that our wealth is to be used to minister to the needs of our people rather than to assist ourselves and others in preparations for mutual extermination.
This is not the time to go in any great detail into the many defects and abuses which we are here to remedy, but may I suggest that there are one or two things we should bear in mind. In my own experience in the commercial life of this country for about twenty-five years I have observed some glaring defects. While we all recognize the complexity of our problems and that one nation alone cannot solve the world's problems, yet there are measures that can be taken here in Canada as a first step towards the removal of these abuses.
_ I am familiar with the affairs of a town in western Canada which in 1912 to 1915 borrowed $80,000 on long term debentures. Those debentures were issued at a discount; from the proceeds of the sale the people received $71,000. Prior to 1937 they have paid back $95,000 and still owe $150,000. That is not an isolated case, Mr. Speaker; that illustrates the effect of one of the greatest drains upon our purchasing power in Canada. I could apply the same principle to the Canadian National Railways. The interest on the stocks and bonds of that company, if it averaged five per cent and were paid regularly for twenty years, would be equal to the entire capital invested in that company, and still we would have to pay it over and over and over again, every generation. That is one of the problems to which I think we should give careful consideration at this session, and I have no doubt that opportunities will arise to permit that to be done.
Another abuse is gambling in futures on the grain exchange. I have before me a short
51052-22}
article taken from Common Sense for January, 1938, in which the writer, Mr. Ernest Mac-dougall, points out:
The futures market is a parasitical overgrowth on the body of the commodity market. The annual business of the grain futures gambling market runs to four billion dollars, and the commissions of grain futures brokers amount to one hundred million dollars a year. Divided among five hundred futures brokers, that is a prize worth fighting for! And this has nothing to do with the commissions paid on the actual sale and delivery of actual commodities.
I hope to have something more to say on that question a little later on in the session. Broadly speaking, I think the answer to our problem is increased production. I have under my hand a short article from another issue of Common Sense, that of November, 1937, by Congressman Allen of Pennsylvania. I should like to put on Hansard his conclusions with regard to the situation across the line, because it closely approximates our own. He says:
In spite of the earnest attempts of the Roosevelt administration the share of the workers in the national income produced was less in 1936 than in 1929. The owners of our industrial machinery, however, pocketed $4,573,000,000 in dividends in 1936 or an increase of 50 per cent over 1935. During the same time the total income of the workers was held down to an increase of only 14 per cent. Commodities are manufactured to be sold. They cannot be sold so long as people do not have sufficient income to buy them. In this machine age mass consumption is a prime requisite. Under the conditions described above we have stifled our own customers. They are helpless. At the same time huge profits have been directed into the pockets of a small number of our people whose consuming power is limited and whose surplus wealth is invested, if at all, in new mechanical equipment designed to produce a constantly increased amount of goods which our people cannot consume. The abuse of technological improvements is constantly threatening to make the machine a curse instead of a blessing to labour. It has brought unemployment and poverty when it could bring security and abundance. Much of our liberal legislation, intended to eliminate unemployment, raise wages and increase production, has been thwarted. We have in many respects actually played into the hands of those whose privileges we sought to curb. Instead of halting them we have set in motion the very forces that nearly ruined us in 1929.
Scarcity and contraction are impossible in thi9 machine age. No longer can we "plough under" our labour force, and mechanical equipment. We must expand our output and then make that output available to those who need it. The creation of more wealth alone can solve the economic problem of the underprivileged without inflicting hardships on other classes of our people.
I think we have some food for serious thought there.
340	COMMONS
The Address-Mr. Rowe (Athabaska)
Now, Mr. Speaker, before sitting down I should like to suggest that there are steps we can take in Canada. We can plan for the utilization of our resources to a far greater extent than we are doing. I have before me a copy of Wonders of World Engineering, for August. 1937, published in London, England. At page 730 I read:
The hydrogen gas is made from coke in a special plant and the total raw coal consumption at Billingham for the 100,000 tons of petrol made directly from coal each year is
500,000	tons.
That shows that with our great coal resources in Alberta, in addition to the raw oil in the Turner valley and the oil contained in the Athabaska tar sands we have great quantities of oil in our coal, and that oil already is being commercially extracted.
The other day I read in the Regina Star of January 22 a proposal for-the irrigation of the western prairies. The writer, Mr. Cleugh, suggested that by piping streams such as the Bow river and the Saskatchewan river high enough upstream, we could run the water by gravity over the prairies and turn them into a garden. I suggest that we should divert some of the $50,000,000 a day used by the world last year in the construction of armaments with which to destroy the people of the world into a .constructive channel such as that, in order to feed the world. If the world spent fifteen billion dollars last year on armaments, this means that $50,000,000 was spent every day for 300 days, taking out two weeks for holidays and every Sunday, when we mocked off to pray for peace. We might livert that money and that labour into a instructive channel and show the people of the world that we are ready to cooperate in feeding them and supplying their wants rather than in preparing to destroy them.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I wonder what we are going to say to the young people and the unemployed in this country. As the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Cold-well) said the other day, I feel that we should stay here until, working together, we have formulated a plan that will be the beginning of the solution of the problems which confront us. So far as I am concerned I do not think parliament should prorogue until some plan of that kind has been found.
I am confronted now with the question of how I shall vote on this motion and the amendment thereto. I have been forced to indulge in some destructive criticism; but I am sure members of the government appre-

ciate the fact that these defects and abuses exist, and no doubt they are as anxious as I am to solve them.
The question in regard to the amendment is this: Is it a sound principle to suggest that free trade could ever conceivably cause friction among the nations of the world? My idea of trade is that we should export only that surplus required to bring in those goods which we cannot produce advantageously within Canada. To make effective our domestic market; to rearrange and bring up the wages of farmers and workers in the country so as to absorb more of the domestic market, and to undertake to remove from our trade arrangements with other nations retaliatory and discriminatory tariffs which hamper and thwart other nations from developing their own economy, must, in my view, be the ideal and ultimate goal of world trade.
I cannot conceive of free trade being the cause of war. I will grant hon. members this, that under our present competitive price and profit system difficulties do exist; but I have been a student of international affairs for some time, and I am most anxious to do everything possible to alleviate and disarm the fears of people in other countries. Therefore, on that one point alone, I have decided to vote with the government.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on this occasion I wish to confine my remarks to a paragraph from the speech from the throne, the implications of which I consider fundamental to successful democratic government in Canada. I refer to the paragraph concerning contemplated amendments to the British North America Act. What I have to say on this important subject I shall say not from a partisan point of view or even as the representative, particularly, of the electors in my constituency. Rather I shall speak as a Canadian representing the Canadian people.
Since elected to this house I have been deeply interested in the constitutional position obtaining in Canada. I am sorry to be compelled to relate that my investigations into the subject have sadly disillusioned me on many matters. I hope it will not be considered presumptuous for a back-bencher, without law school diplomas, to express opinions on a subject as intricate as constitutional law. I approach the question more from the point of view of the average citizen who wishes to know the why and wherefore of all he sees and hears.
Speaking on this question the right hon. the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) referred to the methods employed by other British dominions, notably Australia and South Africa,

in amending their constitutions. After reading the constitution of the Commonwealth of Australia, and the method by which the people of Australia amend it, I wondered, since the enactment of the Statute of Westminster of 1931 which made Canadian citizens politically independent of the imperial parliament, why we have not the same privilege with respect to a constitution.
I am pleased to note that the speech from the throne mentions the Statute of Westminster, and indicates that it is being recognized as an effective measure.
In considering the present constitutional position in Canada I find myself faced with the situation referred to by Professor Keith in his book, The Sovereignty of the British Dominions. At page 201 he says:
Those who claim autonomy for Canada naturally cannot acquiesce in a position under which the supremacy of the imperial parliament is insistent and undeniable. A sovereign state whose constitution can only be altered by another power is a contradiction in adjecto.
The more one studies these matters, the more contradictions he finds. In order to have an intelligent understanding of our constitutional status I have spent considerable time in making a study of the history surrounding the passing of the British North America Act. All the evidence I have been able to gather compels me to entertain grave doubts as to whether or not any individual member of this assembly has authority, or whether as a group we have authority to legislate as a parliament. I have discovered what in my opinion are discrepancies both in the British North America Act and in the historical record. I trust I am doing an acceptable service in bringing some of these matters to the attention of the house, the legal authorities in which may be able to provide me with the necessary enlightenment.
In Hansard of April 1,	1936, the leader of
the opposition	is quoted	as	saying that	thepreamble is an important part of a bill. I wish to discuss the preamble to the British North America Act, as we find it in the printed copies.	In order	to	indicate the	importance of a	preamble	I	shall quote	the
observations of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) and the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan) in the debate which took place on the wheat bill.
I quote from Hansard of April 1, 1936.
Mr. Bennett: Parliament for the first time within my knowledge . . .is asked to pass a preamble . . . that is not supported by documents attached as schedules to the bill. A preamble is rather an important part of a bill. ... A preamble is useful when you are
The Address-Mr. Kuhl
endeavouring to interpret the legislation in respect to it. .	.	. In private bills it is
essential to establish by competent testimony every fact inserted in the preamble. . . .
Mr. Mackenzie King: My right hon. friend will I think, agree that there is no better authority on legislative methods and forms than Sir Courtenay Ubert, Parliamentary Council to the Treasury. At page 269 of his treatise "Legislative Methods and Forms," I find the following with respect to preambles:
As. a rule a preamble is unnecessary in a public bill. Where the object is merely to describe briefly the reason for and the intended effect of the proposed legislation, the object can often be better obtained by prefixing a short explanatory memorandum to the bill, ouch a memorandum should state concisely the e^tmg law, the reasons for amendment and the effect of the proposed amendments. A local bill must always have a preamble, the recital in which must be proved/'
Mr. Cahan: And they must be proved.
Mr. Mackenzie King: My hon. friend says they must be proved. That is correct. . . . Then the only remaining point at issue is whether or not the preamble contains an exact recital of facts.
Mr. Bennett:	And whether it has been
proven . . .
I would direct the attention of hon. members to a particular statement of the leader of the opposition as reported at page 1695 where he states:


	ujneas uie preamoi
before the committee, the bill fails.
The gist of the argument would seem to be, then, that the language in the preamble must be consistent; the recital of the words must be in accordance with the facts, and unless the preamble can be proven the bill fails. Let us in the light of these facts examine the preamble to the British North America Act. Let us ask of the preamble these questions: Is the language in the preamble consistent? Is the recital of the words in the preamble in accordance with facts? Can the preamble be proven? Was the preamble proven?
In order to make sure that we are not starting out on a false premise I wish to submit a few historical facts which will substantiate that the British North America Act is a private act, or a public act resembling a private act. As the British North America Act did not affect the entire empire, but was restricted to the three colonies enumerated, and further restricted in its scope to north America, it was a private bill in its relation to the parliament by which it was enacted. Sir John A. Macdonald, in his letter of July 18, 1889, to Lord Knutsford, said this:
The union was treated by them much as if the British North America Act were a private bill uniting two or three English parishes.
The Address-Mr. Kuhl

Let us now turn to the first question on the preamble: Is the language in_ the preamble consistent? Before proceeding with that question I should like to read the preamble to the British North America Act. I hold in my hand a photostatic copy of the preamble to that act, which reads as follows:
An act for the union of Canada, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, and the government thereof, and for purposes connected therewith.
Whereas the provinces of Canada, Nova Scotia, and New Brunswick have expressed their desire to be federally united into one dominion under the crown of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland, with a constitution similar in principle to that of the United Kingdom;
Before we can determine whether or not the language in the preamble is consistent, there are two terms in the preamble which, I think, we must define. Those are "federally united" and "one dominion." Are these terms synonymous, or are they the antithesis of each other? Bouvier, in his law dictionary, says of the words "federal government" that it consists of "a union or confederation of sovereign states, created either by treaty,^ or by the mutual adoption of a federal constitution."
Doctor Ollivier, law clerk of the House of Commons, at page 85 of the evidence of the special committee on the British North America Act in 1935, says this:
A confederation is a union of independent and sovereign states bound together by a pact or a treaty for the observance of certain conditions dependent upon the unanimous consent of the contracting parties, who are free to withdraw from the union.
It is quite apparent, Mr. Speaker, from these definitions that the status of sovereignty must precede confederation and that a federal union can be consummated only by the mutual consent of contracting states, adopting a constitution.
Now as to the term "dominion." What is a dominion? Is a dominion the same as a federal union? Before the discovery of America by Christopher Columbus the term dominion was used to denote a state or country that was dominated by the imperial parliament. Wales is called a "dominion" in the Acts of Henry VIII as in article 25 of the Treaty of Union, 1707. The Isle of Man was also known as a dominion. Newfoundland, the first colony of England in America, was a dominion founded by Sir Humphrey Gilbert in 1583. Virginia, founded by Sir Walter Raleigh, was a dominion, and is known to-day by the name of "The Old Dominion" in the United States of America.

Section 18, paragraph 3, of the Interpretation Act of 1889 says this:
The expression "colony" shall mean any of Her Majesty's dominions. . . .
We see, then, that a dominion was nothing more than a colony. Do these definitions not indicate that a federal union and a dominion are opposed in nature; that one is the antithesis of the other? How then could the provinces of Canada, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick be federally united into one dominion? Is this not a positive contradiction? Furthermore, how could a colony have a constitution similar in principle to that of the United Kingdom?
The next question we were to consider was, Is the recital of the words in the preamble in accordance with facts? Did the provinces express the desire to be federally united into one dominion? Before discussing the desire of the provinces I believe it would be well to indicate the constitutional status of the provinces before the British North America Act was passed. As all hon. members know, the province of Canada governed herself for more than twenty-five years prior to the passing of the British North America Act, by the Act of Union of 1840. I wish to quote a few sections from the Act of Union to indicate the nature of the government at that time.
3. Her Majesty shall have power by and with the advice and consent of said legislative council and assembly to provide for the peace, order and good government of the province of Canada .	.	. and that such laws being
passed by the said legislative council and assembly and assented to by Her Majesty or assented in Her Majesty's name by the governor general of the province of Canada shall be valid and tending to all intents and purposes within the province of Canada.
44. Taxes shall be levied by Her Majesty in such manner only as shall be directed by any law or laws which may be made by Her Majesty by and with the advice and consent of _ the legislative council and assembly of such province.
61. In this act, unless otherwise expressed therein the words "acts of the legislature of the province of Canada" are to be understood to mean an act of Her Majesty, heirs or successors, enacted by Her Majesty with the advice and consent of the legislative council and assembly of the province of Canada and the words "governor of the province of Canada' are to be understood as comprehending the governor or person authorized to execute the office of governor of the said province.
In 1854 the imperial parliament passed, in response to an address of the legislative assembly, an act to empower the legislature to alter the constitution of the legislative council, imperial act 17-18 Victoria, chapter 118. The first election of councillors took place in the summer of 1856. Twelve members were elected to the legislative council

The Address-Mr. Kuhl
every two years to hold office for eight years and could be reelected. In 1862 the speaker of the legislative council was elected by the members, Sir Allan MacNab being chosen speaker. In the twenty-seven years between 1840 and 1867, during which time Canada enjoyed responsible government, no act of the province was disallowed. Mr. Gladstone in the British Hansard of March 28, 1867, at page 754, states:
We have for a full quarter of a century acknowledged absolutely the right of selfgovernment in the colonies.
The words "federally united" in the preamble are equivalent to the recognition and acceptance by the imperial parliament of the status of Canada, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, that they were free and competent to sign a compact to which they, without coercion, would mutually agree. Now, what was the desire expressed by the provinces? The preamble to the Quebec resolutions states:
The best interests and present and future prosperity of British North America will be promoted by a federal union under the crown.
Section 70 of these resolutions states:
The sanction of the imperial and local parliaments shall be sought for the union of the provinces on the principles adopted by the conference.
The bill drafted in London by the delegates from the provinces, and presented by the Hon. John A. Macdonald to Lord Carnarvon, Secretary of State for the Colonies, contains a reiteration of this desire in the following words:
Whereas the provinces of Canada, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, have expressed their desire to form a federal union under the crown-
In order further to determine the desire expressed by the provinces, let us examine the manner in which the bill was drafted and presented. The act was drafted by the law officers of the crown attached to the colonial office. Lord Carnarvon was chairman. I quote Sir Frederick Rogers, Under Secretary for the Colonies:
They held many meetings at which I was always present. Lord Carnarvon was in the chair, and I was rather disappointed in his power of presidency.
That is taken from Lord Blachford's letters, page 301.
The law officers of the crown drafted the bill to guide the delegates, the title and preamble of which read respectively:
The union of the British North American colonies, and for the government of the united colony.
And the preamble:
Whereas the union of the British North American colonies for purposes of government and legislation would be attended with great benefits to the colonies and be conducive to the interests of the United Kingdom.
This was the desire of the colonial office, and it appears that it prevailed over the desire of the provinces, which read:
Whereas the provinces of Canada, Nova Scotia, and New Brunswick have expressed their desire to form a federal union under the British crown for the purpose of government and legislation, based upon the principles of the British constitution-
Why was Lord Carnarvon chairman of the delegates from Canada, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick? Is this not a violation of natural law?
Consider this: If the British North America Act contained in some measure the desire expressed by the provinces, would it not have been simply a matter of common courtesy on the part of the noble lord who was chairman of the delegates from Canada, and who introduced the bill in the House of Lords, to have at least returned a copy of the act for the consideration and consent of the local legislatures?
Let us now consider how the act was presented. In presenting the bill to the House of Lords, Lord Carnarvon, Secretary of State for the Colonies, and chairman when the bill was being drafted, asserts that:
The bill opens by reciting tbe desire of the several provinces to be federally united.
That will be found in the British Hansard of February 19, 1867, page 559. When presented, the Quebec resolutions were attached to the bill as an enunciation of the motives prompting or impelling the colonial office to present the measure, for on the second reading, on Februaiy 26, Lord Campbell says:
The bill is founded, I believe, on what is termed the Quebec scheme of 1864 .... Our lights indeed may be imperfect upon this part of the subject, and I will not dwell upon it. But one thing is clear: The preamble of the resolution comes before us in full and perfect authenticity.
That will be found in the British Hansard of February 26, 1867, page 1012.
The present preamble as printed was not debated.
The act was not yet printed, as is evidenced by the excerpts from the speeches in the House of Commons. I should like now to quote Mr. Hadfield. as reported at page 1090 of the British Hansard of February 27, 1867:
Mr. Hadfield said be rose to ask of the government why it was the second reading of this bill had been fixed for to-morrow. It was one which affected 4.600.000 of people and upon which great doubts and differences of opinion
The Address-Mr. Kuhl

were entertained. It was not yet printed and was of so important a character that he thought some little time ought to elapse after it was in the hands of the members before it was introduced, in order that some little consultation should take place upon it. He was not at all sure that he should be opposed to it but he certainly required more time to consider it.
On the following day, February 28, at page 1195 of the British Hansard, Mr. Hadfield is reported as follows:
He (Mr. Hadfield) thought that a bill of Bueh great importance ought not to be passed through parliament with such haste. It was read a third time in the House of Lords, only on Tuesday night, and two days after they were called to give it a second reading in that house (Commons). That was a bad precedent to establish and might produce ill ' effect at another time. If the bill had been delayed only for a few weeks, the people of Nova Scotia would have been able to express an opinion upon it. He had not had time to consider either the bill itself or the papers on the subject which had been put into his hands.
I have another quotation which casts light on the manner in which the matter was presented. It will be found in the British Hansard of February 28, 1867, at page 1179. Mr. Bright said:
I have heard there is at present in London a petition complaining of the hasty proceedings of parliament and asking for delay, signed by 31,000 adult males of the province of Nova Scotia, and that petition is in reality signed by at least half of all the male inhabitants of that province. So far as I know, the petition does not protest absolutely against union but against the manner in which it is being carried out by this scheme and bill and by the hasty measures of the colonial office. . . . Nobody pretends that the people of Canada prefer a nominated council to an elective council . . . to put seventy men in that council for life inserts into the whole scheme the germ of a malady which will spread and rvhich before long will require an alteration of this act, and of the constitution of this new confederation. ... I am satisfied . . . that we run a great danger of making this act work ill from almost the beginning. . . . There is no part of the world in my opinion which runs less risk^ of aggression than Canada. .	.	. No political
party in America ever dreamed for a moment of aggression upon Canada or of annexing Canada by force. And therefore every farthing you spend upon fortresses ... is money squandered. through an hallucination we ought to get rid of. . . . For my share I want the population of these provinces to do that which they believe the best for their own interest- remain with this country if they like, in the most friendly manner, or become independent states if they like.
Is it not quite apparent from this evidence, Mr. Speaker, that the desire expressed by the provinces was for a federal union and for nothing but that?

I have searched many records and nowhere have I been able to find that the provinces expressed the desire to be federally united into one dominion. I ask hon. members, Can the preamble to the British North America Act, in the light of this evidence, be said to be an exact recital of facts?
Before answering the last two questions regarding the preamble which I asked in the early part of my address, there is one other question which may very well be answered first: Did the British North America Act do for the provinces what they desired it to do? Or, putting it in other words; Did the provinces of Canada, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick become a confederation or a federal union through the British North America Act? In reply to that question could we not very well ask: Had the provinces federated, would not an agreement or a pact have had to be signed? Had an agreement been signed, would we not have a record of it? Would we not at least have had a certified copy of the act?
The fact is, Mr. Speaker, that notwithstanding that the imperial parliament recognized Canada as being responsible since 1840, Canada was reduced to the position of a colony by the British North America Act. Canada did not become a federal union or a confederation but was demoted to the status of a colony under the name of "dominion." An important piece of evidence on this point is, I believe, a statement by Sir John Bourinot in Canada under British Rule, chapter 8, page 215, in which he says:
It is interesting to know' that in the original draft of the bill the united provinces were called the Kingdom of Canada, but when it came eventually before parliament, they were designated as " the dominion of Canada," and the writer had it from Sir John A. Macdonald himself that this amendment did not emanate from the colonial delegates, but from the imperial ministry.
In order that we might know definitely the constitutional status Canada attained through the British North America Act, the imperial parliament defined the term "dominion" in section 18, paragraph 3 of The Interpretations Act of 1889, which reads:
The expression "colony" shall mean any of Her Majesty's dominions exclusive of the British islands and of British India; and where parts of such dominions are under both a central legislature and local legislatures, all parts under the central legislature shall, for the purpose of this definition, be deemed to be one colony.
Excepting Canada, no country in the empire had a central legislature and local legislatures; therefore, twenty-two years after the enactment of the British North America Act, Can-

The Address-Mr. Kuhl
ada is deemed to be one colony. Prior to 1867 her majesty could act only by and with the advice and consent of the legislative council and assembly of the province of Canada. Members of both the legislative assembly and the legislative council were elected by the people. The members of the legislative council elected their speaker. According to the provisions of the British North America Act, the members of the legislative council are appointed by the governor general. The Speaker is appointed and can be removed at his discretion. Members of the privy council are appointed to aid and advise him and can be removed at his discretion. Canada lost all power of self-government through the British North America Act.
Sir John A. Macdonald protested against the British North America Act while it was being drafted as well as later. If hon. members will take the trouble to refer to Pope's Confederation Documents they will find a written protest of Sir John A. Macdonald's against the British North America Act. In the forepart of the book we find a copy of the draft of the bill, the title of which reads:
Draft of a bill for the union of the British North American colonies, and for the government of the united colony.
Judging from the way in which the page is disfigured, Sir John A. Macdonald was not agreeable to this. Alongside it we find in his own handwriting what he desired, and it reads:
Whereas the provinces of Canada, Nova Scotia, and New Brunswick have expressed their desire to form a federal union for the purposes of government and legislation, based on the principles of the British constitution. . . .
And in a letter to Lord Knutsford, dated July 18, 18S9, Sir John said:
Had a different course been pursued-for instance, had united Canada been declared to be an auxiliary kingdom, as it was in the Canadian draft of .the bill, I feel sure (almost) that the Australian colonies would ere this, have been applying to be placed in the same rank as the kingdom of Canada.
Now, as to the last two questions: Can the preamble be proven? Was the preamble proven? The evidence which I have submitted proves conclusively, I believe, that a dominion and a colony were identical; that to be federally united an agreement must be signed; that no compact or agreement was signed; that to be federally united into one dominion was an impossibility; that the provinces did not express their desire to be federally united into one dominion. I ask, therefore: How can the preamble be proven? Furthermore, if the preamble cannot be proven to-day, how could it have been proven in 1867? My opinion, therefore, based upon the evidence which I have submitted, is similar
to that expressed by the leader of the opposition on the wheat bill of 1936. Speaking to the preamble the leader of the opposition said, as reported at page 1694 of Hansard of 1936:
I do not think the Prime Minister would desire that the house should give its support to a preamble which is not in accordance with the facts. I point out that the language which is employed in this preamble is not even consistent, and is not in accordance with the facts.
That is exactly my opinion with regard to the preamble to the British North America Act. I wish to repeat the statement of the leader of the opposition as reported on page 1695:
. . . in every case, unless the preamble is proven before the committee, the bill fails.
The preamble to the British North America Act was not proven and could not be proven, as it is incapable of proof. Therefore the bill fails. If the foregoing be true, then I submit that the British North America Act is null and void.
To suggest that we refer this evidence to the courts would be in my opinion another way of sidestepping our responsibility in the matter. As it is impossible to submit all the evidence in this debate, I suggest that the house should consider the question in committee of the whole. In order to suggest what must be done under the circumstances to rectify the present situation I wish to quote some evidence given by eminent Canadian constitutional authorities to the special committee on the British North America Act in 1935. Hon. members would do well to take heed of the evidence given by eminent constitutional authorities in Canada. The logical question, after one peruses the evidence, which I have submitted is: Where do we go from here? I believe the answer was very well suggested in the evidence that was given to the committee. Professor Norman McLeod Rogers, now Minister of Labour, was giving evidence at this particular time. As reported at page 116 of the evidence Mr. Cowan asked this question:
You get back to this: your start is another interprovincial conference?
The answer was:
I am afraid it is. I see no feasible alternative.
Hon. Mr. Lapointe:	There is no doubt
about it.
I wish now to quote Doctor W. P. M. Kennedy, professor of Law of the university of Toronto. At page 69 he is reported as follows:
1 think we have got to get away from the idea that the British North America Act is a "contract" or "treaty." I do not want to go into that, but it is true neither in history nor
The Address-Mr. Kuhl

in law. The British North America Act is a statute, and has always been interpreted as a statute. Suppose now we assume that it is necessary to have constituent powers in Canada, power's to change the constitution. (sic) I approach that problem from two angles. First of all	I	want to break	the British NorthAmerica Act up. We have got to ask ourselves,	Is	the dead hand	of the past to	beconstantly laid with numbing effect on the body politic? That is really what it amounts to .	. . If we in Canada are not capable of
interpreting our own constitution we should not have a legislature at all.
I quote now Doctor Skelton, Under-Secretary of State for External Affairs, at page 27:
Now	it	might be said,	Why not trust	togrowth	of	convention or custom altogether	for
the necessary changes in our constitution? The obvious answer, I think, is that the process is too slow, and is applicable only in cases where unanimity has been reached.
And at page 42:
No other country in the world looks to the parliament of another country for the shaping of its constitution. This solution would only be supported if we believe that Canadians are the only people so incompetent that they cannot work out a solution of their constitutional problem, and so biased that they alone among the peoples of the world cannot be trusted to deal fairly with the various domestic interests concerned. . . .
It is not safe to leave the question open and ambiguous indefinitely; for at any time a dispute on a concrete issue may arise.
... To retain permanently the intervention of the parliament of the United Kingdom is either superfluous or dangerous.
Doctor Maurice Ollivier says, at page 55:
Furthermore our constitution is a law adopted by the British parliament exercising its incontestable right of sovereignty towards its colonies. . . . This explains the fact that the British North America Act is not a reproduction of the Quebec resolutions.
I should like now to quote Doctor Beau-;hesne, the worthy clerk of this house. I oelieve Doctor Beauchesne should be highly commended for the very progressive suggestions he made to this committee. They are found at page 125, as follows:
It is quite true that if we apply to the British North America Act the principles followed in the interpretation of statutes it is not a compact between provinces; it is an act of parliament which does not even embody all the resolutions passed in Canada and in London prior to its passage in the British parliament where certain clauses that had not been recommended by the Canadian provinces were added. . . .
The Statute of Westminster has altered our status. . . . What we want is a new constitution.
The new constitution must leave nobody with a grievance.

A spirit of conciliation should predominate. For these reasons, the task must be entrusted to an independent body in which all the elements of the country will be represented.
I want the assembly to sit in a city in the west. It would not be necessary for a delegate to be a member of parliament or of a provincial legislature.
I _ would suggest that the assembly do not sit in Ottawa, in order that it may not have the appearance of being dominated, or even influenced by the dominion power; and, as the western provinces are of such paramount importance in the country, I suggest the best city for the representatives to gather in would be Winnipeg.
Whether our country should be changed from a dominion to a kingdom is also a subject which might be discussed. I would suggest that the country could be called "The Federated States of Canada."
There have been many disputes about provincial rights since 1867 and it seems certain that when a new constitution is drawn up the distribution of federal and provincial powers will have to be modified.
At page 131:
1 submit that appeals to the privy council should be dealt with by our constitution. This method would preserve the principle of taking our cases to the highest tribunal without going out of our own country.
At page 132:
If you will allow me, Mr. Chairman, I will just make another suggestion; if we have a constituent assembly and if we, discuss the making of a new' constitution, I think it is an anomaly that dominion affairs should, to a certain extent, be subject to provincial authority. I would suggest that we have a federal district, taking in about tw-enty-five square miles on each side of the Ottawa river.
And at page 134:
I would not have any minority rights discussed. There is nothing more dangerous in Canada than a discussion of minority rights. A discussion of them would wreck the whole constituent assembly.
I think the time is ripe for a change in the constitution. I do not thirtk you would need much publicity in order to draw to the attention of the people of this country that the British North America Act is inadequate.
In prefacing my remarks I stated that I was speaking not from a partisan point of view or as representing particularly my constituency in Alberta, but as a Canadian representing the people of Canada. I appeal particularly to hon. members from Ontario and Quebec. From Ontario came William Lyon Mackenzie; from Quebec, Papineau, who were exiled from Canada for their patriotism, and whose followers were imprisoned and hanged. But by their efforts from 1835 to 1837, Ontario and Quebec achieved the right to govern themselves, by the Act of Union of 1840. The right of self-government was taken from Canadians by the British North America Act. No

The Address-Mr. Barber
longer do we elect our upper house, or the Speaker of that house, and to-day under this act our enactments are subject to the power of disallowance. The prima facie evidence which I have presented to the house to-day stands upon the record until it is refuted. How, may I ask, is the government to proceed to amend an act the preamble of which cannot be proven? This is manifestly impossible.
I take pleasure, therefore, in placing myself on record in favour of the amendment to the address in reply to the speech from the throne, so far at least as any reference in the speech from the throne concerns an amendment to the British North America Act. The Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) and the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) will agree with me when I suggest an interprovincial conference, as they suggested in 1935. That there was no confederation is attested by Doctor Ollivier, Doctor Kennedy, Doctor Skelton and Doctor Beauchesne, also by the incontestable fact that there was no certified copy of the act in Canada, showing that the provinces of Canada were not consulted. In closing, I desire to record my approval of the suggestion made by Doctor Beauchesne, that the provinces choose members for an assembly to construct a constitution, and that the country could be called "The Federated States of Canada."

Mr. Speaker, not being a constitutional lawyer or even a member of the legal profession I shall not undertake to deal with the last speaker's observations. I shall leave that to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe), who some day may reply.
This debate is a free-for-all, the first of the session. I think from the beginning until to-night it has been a real free-for-all. I am going to use this opportunity, not to dwell very long on the speech from the throne but to bring to the attention of the government some matters which in the interest of Canada, I believe, should be dealt with at this session. I think it is generally understood that the speech of his excellency presented at the opening of the session is a means taken by the government to place before parliament the program of legislation which it is intended to deal with during the session. In the first session following the election there was perhaps some excuse for not bringing in a very heavy program to carry out the pledges of the Liberal party during the 1935 election. Then the second session was very brief in order that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) might be able to represent Canada at the coronation and at the imperial conference.
But, let me tell the government that the people of Canada expect some action during the present session. Almost three years have passed and nothing has been done to remedy conditions in this country.
Now let us look at this program of legislation and see if there is anything to relieve the serious economic condition that exists among the great masses of our people. It is true that we are to consider the amendment of the British North America Act, if the cooperation of the provinces is forthcoming. We are to deal with the elections and franchise acts. The government proposes to do something about the export of power. The authority of the board of railway commissioners is to be extended. It is hoped that negotiations may so progress as to render it possible to submit to parliament a new trade agreement with the United States.
That, Mr. Speaker, is the program, and I am afraid the Canadian people can take very little comfort from it. I believe they will be very much disappointed when they learn through the press that in the third session of this parliament this is the program brought before parliament by this government to deal with our problems. But we are told in this same speech, "Oh, everything is lovely. Canada has once more returned to prosperity. Look at our export trade." How many times we have heard that during this debate. The other night the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Euler) told us that we are now in fourth place among the exporting nations. "Look at our revenues; they have reached a new high level. As a result more money has poured into the treasury than in any year in the history of this country."
Yes, not only has our export trade increased during the last twelve months, but there has been a steady increase in our export trade ever since the low dip of the depression in 1933. It is true that there was a change of government during that time, but it is some comfort to a few of us on this side of the house to know that the policy of the previous administration has been very closely adhered to. The Ottawa agreements, negotiated by a Conservative government and so vigorously opposed by hon. gentlemen opposite, are mainly responsible for the progress Canada has made in selling her products abroad. Through those agreements the greatest market in the world was opened to Canadian producers. The opening of other channels of trade was bound to follow and added to that increase.
Yes, our statistics show that exports from Canada have increased to a considerable extent during the last twelve months. Natural
The Address-Mr. Barber

products and raw materials have been mainly responsible for that increase, raw materials to be consumed by the warring nations and the other great nations in their armament programs. I wonder what would happen to this great export trade of which we boast if this year the nations of the world should cease war and agree to disarm. What would we have in this country? We would present a very fine example of a nation that could not live by export trade alone. Let me put another question: How can this country ever expect to put its great army of unemployed to work if we continue to export our raw materials and buy back manufactured products, giving employment to people of other countries and denying employment to our own people?
Yes, our revenues have reached a new level. As has been pointed out in the debate, these revenues are raised entirely by taxation, so in other words the people of Canada have this year contributed more money in the way of taxes than in any other year in the history of Canada. The Prime Minister tells us this indicates that the country is prosperous; that the $401,000,000 of revenue derived by taxation this year supplies the answer to the amendment which has been moved by my right hon. leader (Mr. Bennett). The Prime Minister also said that these increased revenues indicate the degree of relative prosperity in Canada compared with what it has been in the past. Prosperity! Has prosperity reached our people when at the present time about one-eleventh of our total population is on relief and the average income of the great mass of our people is not sufficient to maintain a decent standard of living? What about the farmers of our country? Are they prosperous? What about the labourers? Are they enjoying prosperity? What about the small business men who have been the backbone of many communities throughout this country? They have been forced on the streets in these last few years by combines and corporations. Is it any wonder that we have a demand from a large section of our people for a change in our system? Is it any wonder that some are looking to social credit and others to socialism as advocated by my friends to my left, or that some are even grasping communism and fascism as a way out? We talk about fighting these isms. Well, I would like to say to the government that the way to fight these isms that we dread so much to-day is not by padlock laws, militia or police forces or amendments to the criminal code. The way to fight these things is to remove the evils of our present system; then these isms will disappear.

The people of this country took the Prime Minister at his word during the election campaign. He said that unemployment was a national responsibility; that he would wage a great battle against the moneyed powers. Almost three years have passed. This government has not assumed responsibility for unemployment, and the battle against the moneyed powers has not commenced; not a single gun has been fired. I urge upon the Prime Minister, who has had long experience in public life, who possesses outstanding ability and who is surrounded by able advisers, to direct his efforts towards measures to be brought in during the present session for the purpose of correcting the evils of our economic system.
Dealing with taxation, Mr. Speaker, I want to give one example of how these taxes are applied and how unfair they are in many instances. In the constituency which I have the honour to represent we have several large industries, among them what we call the small fruit industry. Strawberries and raspberries are grown in large quantities and shipped both in the fresh state and in what is called the processed form. In some years we may have extra large crops or weather conditions may be such that we cannot ship in the fresh state. Those berries must be taken care of, and the result has been the erection of jam factories, expensive buildings equipped with expensive machinery. They produce a very fine product, the pure berry and the pure sugar, but lo and behold, that agricultural industry is taxed thirty-one per cent by the federal government, including the sugar taxes and the eight per cent sales tax! I am sorry the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) is not in his seat, because I wanted to bring this matter particularly to his attention. I believe there is no other manufactured or semi-manufactured commodity that pays such an exorbitant tax. The question is: Why should the berry industry be singled out from all other agricultural industries to carry this heavy and unjust burden? Why does not the sales tax apply on honey, maple sugar, maple syrup, cheese, butter, canned milk and similar agricultural products? Why does the total taxation on an imported product which is competitive with the jam-I refer to peanut butter-amount to only sixteen per cent, while the jam beans a tax of thirty-one per cent?
When these people sell fresh berries or berries processed in what is known as sulphur dioxide solution they do not pay any of these taxes. When a merchant or a wholesaler sells sugar in any quantity he does not pay a sales tax. But just as soon as a man goes to work and erects an expensive building, equips

The Address-Mr. Barber
it with expensive machinery and employs hundreds of people-yes, thousands are employed throughout Canada in the industry- to combine fresh berries with sugar to make jam, he is compelled to pay eight per cent sales tax. I shall leave the matter there, trusting that the Minister of Finance will correct this when it comes to his attention in preparing his budget.
A great deal has been said about the increased radio licence fee. X shall not spend much time upon it, simply to say, on behalf of radio owners and dealers in my constituency I protest against the increased licence fee. If we have an increase to $2.50 this year, we may expect that the corporation will make an effort to increase it to $4 or $5 next year. I believe the matter should be investigated and given a little more consideration, and the business of the corporation should be looked into before permission is given to increase the fee.
One further point I should like to bring to the attention of the Minister of Trade and Commerce. A number of producers in British Columbia have been a great deal concerned over reports which have reached them to the effect that the preferences they now enjoy under the Ottawa agreements may be disturbed, and that in the negotiation of the Anglo-American trade arrangements Canada might agree to an extension to United States producers of the preference on such commodities as apples, lumber and fish. The Minister of Trade and Commerce has charged that the leader of the opposition has been responsible for the fear created. I do not think it is necessary to quote the minister's speech in that regard.

Let me tell the minister that long before the statement was made by my leader the United States press carried a statement to the effect that under their trade arrangement with the United Kingdom their producers would receive preferences similar to those given Canada on lumber, fish and apples.
