According to the press of the United Kingdom it will be necessary to .make some changes in the Ottawa agreements, but Canada and other countries will be consulted before those changes are made.
Let me refer to a statement of the minister when, in concluding his observations he said, as reported at page 300 of Hansard:
This government is not so inept, so unwise or so unpatriotic as to sacrifice the interests of the producers of Canada, whether they be agricultural or industrial, for any reason whatsoever.
Does that statement stand good with respect to concessions from Canada under the Anglo-American trade agreement? I wonder if the minister would make a statement on that point, or was he referring only to a trade agreement between Canada and the United States?

I fear there is little comfort to be taken from that statement. There is another matter to which I should like to draw the attention of the government.	I believe the matter I have in
mind, namely soldier settlement, comes under the Department of Mines and Resources. I notice on the order paper a resolution urging that the amendment which has been in force for the last two years be renewed for another period. I should not think it necessary to have a resolution on the order paper to urge upon the government the necessity of the amendment. As hon. members know, that amendment refers to the dollar-for-dollar bonus. May I say to the minister that that is the soldier's only hope of reducing his indebtedness. Eighty-three per cent have taken advantage of it. I should hope to see on the order paper one of these days an amendment continuing the provision for another two years.
Sometimes I think our greatest handicap in British Columbia is distance; we are far away from the centre of Canada, far removed from the seat of government. That great distance creates several problems, one of which the farmers in British Columbia have been trying for some time to get the government to solve. I refer to the cost of transporting grain and grain products from the prairie provinces to British Columbia. This problem is not new to the House of Commons, because to my knowledge we have had it before us for the last ten or twelve years. In connection with the cost of transporting grain a charge of discrimination arises. At this time I shall not go into details in the comparison of rates, because those rates have been placed on Hansard in previous sessions by members from British Columbia, irrespective of party.
Evidence has been submitted to show that not only are the consumers in British Colum-
The Address-Mr. Barber

bia called upon to pay a rate higher than that on similar mileage from prairie points to the east, but also more than double the rate applying to grain shipped from prairie points to Vancouver for export. For the information of new members may I be permitted to give an illustration of how this works out. Let us take, as an example, a train of sixty cars of grain moving from Edmonton to Vancouver. We shall suppose that fifty of those cars are for export and ten for domestic use. On the fifty cars the rate is twenty cents per hundred pounds but on the ten cars, drawn on the same train, the people of British Columbia are penalized to the extent of forty-one cents per hundred pounds. In other words, the freight charge is $4 per ton on the fifty cars for export and S8.30 per ton on similar grain to be used by the farmers in British Columbia.
My reason for bringing the matter to the attention of the government is this: The Liberal party is pledged to remove this differential. Between 1930 and 1935, when this matter was brought before parliament by the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid), he received the solid support of the Liberal party, then occupying the seats to your left, Mr. Speaker. During the election of 1935 the hon. member, quite in good faith, told the electors that if they would elect him and if the Liberal party were returned to power the reduction would take place. Well, the hon. member was elected; the Liberal party was returned with the largest majority ever given to a party in this country; this is the third session, and the differential still remains.

As the Liberal party is pledged to this reduction I wish to make a suggestion to the minister, because I know he does not favour the method by which the hon. member for New Westminster is undertaking to secure the removal of this differential. In 1933, when this matter was urged upon the government of the day, the minister's predecessor, the Hon. Dr. Manion. took action. He called in the heads of the two railways and asked them to have their officers sit in with representatives of the four western provinces and try to work out some reduction on feed grain for domestic use in British Columbia. This was done, and a rate of thirty cents per hundred pounds on certain grades of wheat, oats and barley went into effect on March 10, 1933. That rate is still in effect. Unfortunately mill feeds were not included. Who was to blame I do not know. The matter was decided at the con-
[Mr. Barber.J
ference. This reduction means $2.30 per ton to the farmers and poultrymen of our province, and they have received the full benefit of it. According to a statement I received from the railway companies, at the end of 1935 it meant savings to the farmers amounting to $121,209. Two years have passed since then; I have not the figures up to date; but I think it is safe to say that it has meant a saving to the farmers of three hundred to three hundred and fifty thousand dollars during that time. If the concession had included mill feeds, of which we use a great deal more than we use of these feed grains, the saving would have been just that much more. Today, when dairy products are very low in price, people in the lower mainland of British Columbia are paying $1.75 for a hundred pound sack of bran and $2.60 a sack for oil cake. I mention oil cake because, if we could get a reduction on oil cake we could displace that soya bean meal which is being sold there.
Let me tell the minister that dealers in the lower mainland of British Columbia are buying American wheat, No. 2, a better grade of wheat than they are getting in the feed grains from the prairies, and are selling it to poultry-men and farmers in the Fraser valley at fifty cents per ton less than the price of the Canadian product. My suggestion to the minister is that he follow the same course, talk it over with the heads of the two railways, and see if it would not be possible to have another conference, consisting of representatives of the two railroads and of the four western provinces, to ascertain whether something could not be done further to reduce this differential and to include mill feeds and oil cake in that list.

The consumers would think it worth while. It would certainly make a great difference to the dairymen and farmers of our district. Why should we continue to be discriminated against in the difference between twenty and forty-one cents a hundred on the same grain hauled by train to Vancouver? I think the railways should give us a cut on it, at any rate down to twenty-five cents.
In the matter of railway rates distance is certainly a handicap. This brings to mind another matter which I wish to bring up for the information of the house. I do not suppose the minister can do anything with this. But prior to the end of last October motor cars were shipped into our province at the flat rate of $120 a car, which we thought and I think hon. members generally would consider, a fairly high rate. Later on, behold like a shot out of the blue, on November 1 new rates went into effect-a rate of $4.87 per hundred pounds! That means that on the lighter type of car weighing 2,900 pounds the rate is increased from $120 to $141.23; on a car that weighs about 3,300 pounds the former charge of $120 has been increased to $160.71; on a car running about 3,500 pounds, a beautiful car which we should all like to own, the rate, which was $120, is now $170.45. On trucks the flat rate was the same, namely $120. A new rate of $4.12 per hundred pounds has been put into effect. Thus, a truck weighing 4,400 pounds, which was shipped into our province from the east for $120, now pays $18128, or a 50 per cent increase in freight rates. The charge on a truck weighing 3,700 pounds is increased from $120 to $152.44. These amounts do not include decking and loading charges, which are extra. The result is that a large number of people are coming east, buying or taking delivery of their cars here and driving them back, and some firms are negotiating to have their cars brought through the Panama canal to Vancouver.
In this, I hope not too lengthy a part I have taken in this debate, I have tried to bring some matters to the attention of the government. The Minister of Finance was out of the chamber when I referred to the tax, but I know he will look it up in Hansard and will give it serious consideration.

I understand that I am the last speaker before the vote is to be taken. I do not intend, therefore, to exceed my time. I shall be as brief as I possibly can.
The speech from the throne provides, of course, an opportunity for the discussion of many items. I do not propose to deal in detail with any number of them, but I might remark at this point that I do not recall any similar debate wherein so many ministers spoke so early in the session in defence of the functions of their departments, and I must say that, listening to those speeches, I have enjoyed and have been gratified at the high level which they have attained. I believe their speeches influenced the quality of the contributions by other hon. members, in that they also attained a very high level. This debate will compare worthily with any previous debates of this kind and is in accordance with the best traditions of the house. I know that most of the ministers who took part in this debate were drawn into it by the highly provocative speech made by the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett). He gave some very hard knocks, and I think he also received some. But he seems to thrive upon them.
It is inevitable that in this house constituted as it is, with representatives from all over the dominion, representing differing and conflicting views, there must of necessity be some differences of opinion. But when the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Heaps) the other day referred in gleeful tones to the many protesting speeches that were made on this side of the house and also from some on the other side immediately to your left, Mr. Speaker, in what we affectionately and euphoniously call " the rump," I think he overlooked the fact that there is no Liberal party worthy of the name but must have in its ranks members, be the number large or small as it may happen, who appear to be somewhat rebellious and impenitent speakers. It would not be a Liberal party if there were not differences and distinctions of opinion. The life and health of any Liberal party depend upon helpful criticism to build up and construct Liberal policies. I have endeavoured many a time to convert my hon. friend from Winnipeg North, for he is one of my particular friends, but in a conflict between a Jew and a Scot I do not know who is likely to win. I am hoping that some day I may be able to give him knowledge of this fact, that the Liberal party does not prohibit free thought or free speech, nor yet does it eject by executive decree any of the rebellious and impenitent members of the party.
The Address-Mr. Glen

I am going to deal first with one or two matters that are more local than general, so far as the Dominion of Canada is concerned. Last summer my constituency of Marquette, along with parts of Dauphin and Brandon, suffered from the drought, not perhaps to the same extent as Saskatchewan, but still considerably so, and these territories in Manitoba affected by the drought were all west of the Assiniboine river and extending up to the Saskatchewan boundary, and continuing for miles along that boundary. I would not have referred to it had it not been for the fact that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) explained in his speech the other day why no federal assistance was given to these municipalities in Manitoba.
I took the position that we were suffering from the drought and that federal assistance should be given. I had had surveys made of these municipalities and of the conditions prevailing, and they were just as bad as conditions in many of the municipalities adjacent to the one hundred per cent drought area in Saskatchewan. I had officers of the minister's own department come into my constituency, and with them we travelled through it to see the conditions and discuss what the remedy should be. Unfortunately for me my summer was wasted because I was not able to convince the Minister of Agriculture that he should give assistance to my constituency.
The position taken by the federal government was that Manitoba had had the best crop in several years, and in consequence they thought that province was in a position to take care of its own relief. I cannot agree with that. In the adjoining municipalities in Saskatchewan, which are not one whit worse off in the way of crops than my constituency, I find that the farmers there are receiving from the federal government assistance in the way of feed and fodder, and they must in the future be also supplied with seed. They are in no worse condition than their more unfortunate neighbours on the Manitoba side of the boundary, and I think assistance should equally be given to Manitoba, particularly because, as I shall point out a little later, Manitoba is in no position to give the relief I have requested.
The reeve of one of these municipalities wrote telling me of conditions in his municipality, and of how they were able to look across the line and see the adjoining municipalities in Saskatchewan given free feed and fodder, and ultimately they will receive seed as well. He says that he does not begrudge these farmers that assistance and relief, and I agree wholly in what he says; they need that relief. But I must say that they are a

good deal more fortunate than their unfortunate brothers on the Manitoba side, who are receiving no assistance from this government. I felt it was my duty to bring these facts before the house-they have all been submitted already to the department-and if any of the facts I have given are not correct I am anxious that there should be an inspection of the territory, which I am sure will reveal conditions to be more grievous than I have described them in my statement here to-night.
Now I wish to deal with the other question, the inability of Manitoba to finance its own relief, and in that connection I propose to deal with the status of that province within confederation with respect to tariffs.
We had a visit of the Rowell commission in Winnipeg, and let me say, Mr. Speaker, that I deeply deplore the strictures that were passed by the leader of the opposition on the personnel of that commission. I think the right hon. gentleman did a disservice to Canada in making those strictures. I am quite sure that none of the members of that commission accepted their onerous and responsible posij tions except from the very highest patriotic motives. I could not understand any man being willing to assume an obligation so onerous and responsible as these gentlemen have done without being actuated wholly by a desire to help Canada and to conduct their investigation entirely devoid of any spirit of partisanship. I do not know any of the members of that commission personally except Doctor Dafoe, and for those who do not know him I am bound to say this, that not only is he the most distinguished journalist in Canada to-day, but his contributions to Canadian policy at home and abroad have been so outstanding, and his individuality and capacity for independent thinking so striking throughout his long life, that I believe no man in Canada is more preeminent than he to assume that obligation, which I am perfectly satisfied he assumed with great reluctance.
The leader of the opposition in his speech deplored the disunity in Canada at the present time. I am bound to say that in my opinion he has contributed to that disunity, for he has raised in the minds of people questions with regard to, I shall not say the integrity, because that is perhaps not the correct word, but at all events the usefulness of the commission which has been appointed. Statements have been made which it might have been better if they had never been made. We are now familiar in Canadian life with that sinister word "axis." We have forces being joined to-day in some parts for the

The Address-Mr. Glen
purpose of combating other parts of the country. The leader of the opposition is not wholly devoid of blame in the strictures he has made against that commission, who have a real job on their hands, and who, if they apply that partisan spirit of which they are accused, will jeopardize the long and distinguished record which each of these men has attained in the course of a long life in Canada.
Before the Rowell commission in Winnipeg the province of Manitoba submitted its case- a very remarkable one-and it has been attacked surreptitiously, subterraneously, if you will, for having set up the west as against the east. As a representative from Manitoba I say that there was no intention on the part of the province to raise issues as between different sections of the dominion. They were concerned only with the presentation of the case as Manitoba saw it, and perhaps I might use the words of Lincoln, the hundred and twenty-ninth anniversary of whose birth takes place on Saturday-"with malice towards none, with charity to all." That language, I believe, can well be applied to the case submitted by Manitoba. I should like to read from part VII, page 69, of Manitoba's case to show that the province is in no position to finance its own relief, and to justify the request I have made of the government that relief be given to my constituency. At page 69 the following statement is made in paragraph 8 of the summary:
That, other things being as they have been, if Manitoba had so financed its own share of unemployment relief, and those portions of the municipalities' shares which it has had to lend to municipalities, its accumulated deficit in current account for this item alone in the period from April 30, 1930 to April 30, 1937, would be $23,945,637.25. This total is made up, $23,736,570.51 due to the dominion and the public, plus moneys advanced to municipalities out of provincial trust funds to the amount of $209,066.74.
(9)	That Manitoba has, in effect, funded this deficit on current account and has been forced to borrow almost the whole of this from the dominion government because it could not borrow in the money markets.
(10)	That if the dominion government, during this interval, had not continued to lend to Manitoba, the province would have been unable to meet its liabilities.
And at page 71, paragraph 20:
That short of the dominion's taking over the whole administration and financing of unemployment relief, the only practical solution of the problem of financing relief is for the dominion government to distribute amongst the provinces upon a per capita basis of relief population, subject to such reasonable restrictions as to administration as the dominion may

impose, the entire cost of unemployment relief, either as a grant, or as the proceds of a special federal tax upon the whole nation earmarked for relief purposes.
21.	That the financing of relief is quite beyond:
(a)	The present revenue producing capacity of Manitoba.
(b)	The revenue producing capacity which it is possible or desirable for every province in Canada to acquire under a change in the Canadian constitution.
22.	That the present system of financing relief:
(a) Will cause the inevitable bankruptcy of many of the provinces and municipalities of Canada.
Then at page 72, paragraph 24:
That the administration and financing of relief by the dominion is the wisest solution to the relief problem because:
(a)	It would do away with all of the inequitable and subversive effects of the present system of relief administration;
(b)	It would provide a uniform national minimum standard of relief without casting an unfair and unsupportable burden upon any municipality, province or economic area.
In part VIII, page 13, the province makes this statement:
In the Manitoba budget this item appeared only very occasionally and in small amounts prior to the year 1930. From that year up to April 30, 1937, the total cost of relief and relief works in Manitoba was $53,278,775.98. The total cost was divided as follows:
The cost to the dominion	$19,602,697.64
The cost to the province	 18,550.572.12
The cost to the municipalities.. .. 15,125,506.22
It has already been shown elsewhere that
by far the greater part of these expenditures has been met by borrowing. The result is, at April 30, 1937, that the province owed on its relief debt $23,736,570.51, covering both its own costs and moneys borrowed for reloaning to municipalities; the municipalities owe considerable sums to other creditors on their relief debts and, at April 30, 1937, they owed to the provincial government on their account the sum of $4,608,255.74, practically all of which was borrowed by the province from the dominion.	.
In the light of these figures I do not think anyone can successfully contend that Manitoba is in a position to finance its own relief and, therefore, any demand which is made of the federal government should take into account that the 1937 crop in our province, grateful as we are for it, only begins to touch the volume of debt that has accrued in the province and there will have to be a continuation of these crops before Manitoba can be in a position to finance its own relief.
There were some other points brought out in the case submitted to the royal commission. I should like to read one or two state-

The Address-Mr. Glen

merits made by the provincial government with regard to tariffs. At page 18 of part VIII of the submission there appear these words:
At confederation the provinces gave up their jurisdiction over tariff matters to the dominion government. Since that time the tariff policies of the dominion, presumed to be in the interests of the nation as a whole, have worked out to the very great disadvantage of certain provinces.
We have presented to the commission evidence of the burden of this dominion policy on the people of this section of the dominion. The result of our investigation, stated in what we believe to be minimum figures, shows that the burden the dominion tariff places upon the three prairie provinces comes to the staggering total of 58 million dollars per year. This figure is twice as much as the total of all the annual taxes imposed by all three prairie governments combined. It is a heavy price to pay for the privilege of being in confederation.
in the case of Manitoba the tariff policy, as now in effect in Canada, has been found to impose a burden of 15 million dollars per year upon our people. This is an indirect tax of almost unbearable weight. It is seventy-five per cent more than the total of all our provincial taxes which are themselves too heavy. It is almost as much as the total taxes collected by all our municipalities combined. It has for many years imposed a burden exceeding $100 annually on the average farmer in Manitoba. While the tax in itself is burdensome it has the fundamental weakness that the greater part of it is not credited to the dominion government revenues. . . .
It goes on to say that the tariff has thus constituted a heavy load on the primary industries of our province and those of other western provinces.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I have shown the burden which is imposed upon the western provinces as far as tariffs are concerned. It is a gloomy picture so far as I have described it. But I was delighted the other day when I heard the speech of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Euler). I can recall many times when hon. gentlemen opposite called him a protectionist and when the leader of the opposition used to take delight in using that term in order to embarrass him. I think after the minister's speech the other day even the leader of the opposition will have come to the conclusion that that epithet as applied to the minister is entirely a misnomer. In fact, if I were to use any word to describe him I would say that the Minister of Trade and Commerce might be called a realist. He has gone abroad in the world and has seen the effect of trade treaties, and being a realist, he recognizes that after all some of those over here who are called free traders have not been so much out of line. It was also a real delight to find the minister not only grasping with both hands all the

treaties which other countries were willing to conclude with Canada, but indicating that he is still pursuing, and more eagerly than ever, other treaties, because he knows the beneficial effect of them. The increasing revenues of Canada during the past two years, about which so much was said by the last speaker, have demonstrated the value of these treaties. Could anything demonstrate better to the people of Canada that reciprocal trade treaties can have only beneficial results to the countries concerned? The minister indicated in no uncertain terms that even where trade agreements did not include certain items trade in them was also increasing and this country was getting the benefit. I say in the words of an Irishman. More power to the elbow of the Minister of Trade and Commerce.
A parallel picture was given by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) in his speech the other day. He told the story of employment conditions in Canada. It will seem most extraordinary to the mind of the protectionist, but, to the mind of a free trader, a natural consequence, that unemployment has decreased during those two years while foreign trade has been bounding upwards. Both results are linked together. I think the Minister of Labour said that in 1937 as compared with 1936 there was a reduction of 120,000 in the number of unemployed. If that is not an argument in favour of freedom of trade and the removal of restrictions and barriers to trade which some on this side have been advocating for years, then I do not know what an argument is.
I recall that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), either after or during the election campaign, asked the people of this country, whither are we going. Well, I know where we are going if we continue to pursue the path that has been blazed by the Minister of Trade and Commerce, the benefits of which are being shown by the -Minister of Labour. The government has blazed a trail which will convince the people of Canada that freedom from trade restrictions is bound to result in increasing prosperity. They have blazed the trail; all I want the government to do now is to make it a broad highway between us and every country in the world that is willing to trade with us, and I am satisfied that the Liberal party will demonstrate that only by freedom of trade and removal of trade barriers can Canada become one of the most prosperous countries in the world.
Had it not been for the disastrous drought in Saskatchewan; had Saskatchewan been in

The Address-Mr. Johnston (Bow River)
the position, say of Manitoba, or had she produced even half of what she produced in past years, does the country realize that every province would to-day be prosperous, able to balance its budget, and the dominion as a whole would be among the most prosperous countries on the face of the earth? That is what the position would have been but for the drought in Saskatchewan, which caused these ills that we have to remove. Nothing I could say is more pregnant with meaning than the facts submitted by the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the Minister of Labour. While it may be that some of us are more impatient than others, yet we all realize that in the Liberal party lies the only hope for the solution of these problems and the cure of these ills.
I am hoping fervently that the opportunity which is now knocking at the door of the Liberal party will be fully taken advantage of in the legislation to be brought down this session. The results of the government's policy as shown in ever increasing trade are such that the country will be satisfied with having returned in 1935 a government opposed to high protection, of which policy the people of Canada had had bitter experience. I am satisfied that the experience of the two years yet to come before an election will demonstrate to this dominion that through the removal of trade barriers and the promotion of freer trade by the methods adopted by the Minister of Trade and Commerce, Canada will become what she should be, the brightest jewel in the British crown.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I cannot agree with a great many previous speakers who have lauded the speech from the throne so highly. Personally I cannot see in that speech a great deal to be proud of. One thing is certain. As has been stated before in this chamber, one of the greatest problems confronting us is the economic condition of our country, and we are sent here for the purpose of endeavouring to the best of our ability to correct the chaotic conditions under which we live. That is my purpose in speaking to-night. It should be the endeavour of every hon. member not to let time become a factor in closing off any address that might be made in the house when a question so important as the livelihood and very existence of our citizens is under consideration.
We have heard a great deal of praise from the opposite side of the house on the wonderful benefits of the trade agreements. It is
51952-23 j
all very well for a supporter of the government to quote statistics to prove that conditions are improving, but one only has to look about to find with greater surety that conditions are no better than they were a year ago. One thing that makes me wonder is this: In 1935 the party now sitting on the opposite side of this chamber said they were going to remedy these conditions. It has been within their power to do so; they have had the largest majority ever given any party in the house, but I say in all sincerity that so far they have not done anything to any material extent to alleviate those conditions which now exist.
Hon. members speak of foreign trade as being a cure-all for the economic conditions with which we are faced. Well, I am not of that opinion. I agree with some other hon. members, that blasting our way into the markets of the world will never solve our problems. It is not a cure-all, by any manner of means. One of the most important factors we should consider in that connection is the trade within our own boundaries. I have said before in the house, and I have no hesitation in saying it again, that I am not concerned with the tariff. We have only to consider the evidence which has been brought forward in connection with farm machinery to see that the lower the tariff has gone the higher has been the cost of machinery. The tariff in itself is not a factor. I have no objection to the tariff 'being lowered if that will help in any way. Certainly I have no objection to the tariff being raised in order to protect the industries within the confines of this country. But be assured that I do not favour the protection of the profits of the industries of this dominion.
If we were as concerned with the welfare of our people as I believe we should be, we in Alberta would not be faced with the situation that we find to-day in our oil industry. We have one of the greatest potential oil fields in the British Empire, something that should be of great concern to this dominion because of the fact that at present we face one of the most critical times in the history of the empire. We have often thought that we could not be thrown into another world war; yet we are facing that very possibility today. In Alberta we have an oil field which would be of inestimable value to the British Empire if such a tragedy happened; yet what are we doing to assist that great industry? We in Alberta are endeavouring to place that product on the market in eastern Canada. The east has bled the west for many a year, to the extent of millions of dollars. The west has fed the east, but now when we ask for
356	COMMONS
The Address-Mr. Johnston (Bow River)
reciprocation in that regard what do we get? We are not given the slightest bit of consideration. Take the large combines, such as the railways, if you like. When we ask for a reduction in rates they do not even know the cost of transporting a hundred pounds of crude oil for a distance of a hundred miles. When a large concern, such as Imperial Oil, asks them to lower the rate on crude oil to Regina, they do not know how much they can lower the rate without losing money. But when they are faced with the possibility of the construction of a pipe line from the Alberta field to Regina they say to Imperial Oil, "What do you estimate it will cost you to transport that oil?" It was estimated that the cost would be fourteen cents. Then the railways said, "Well, we will charge you nineteen cents. How is that?" They came down just enough to enable them to meet that probable competition. That is not cooperation. We must have something more constructive. If we are endeavouring to find markets for our produce, surely a different attitude might be taken.
Just on this question of trade as a cure-all for the economic ills of the dominion I should like to remind the house that one of the great factors in the improvement, if there has been any improvement, has been the war preparations that have been carried on, as other hon. gentlemen have mentioned already in this debate. I am reminded of a speech that was made here in 1935 by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), as reprinted in Action for January, 1938. This is what the right hon. gentleman said:
I think this country ought to declare that any nation which could be shown to have threatened the peace of the world by violating a pact of collective security should be denied any assistance in the shape of men or muni; tions, should be denied any assistancifTh the nature of food, should be denied any assistance through credit. Our country, small as it is, might well lay down a definite policy in that regard as expressing Canada's attitude toward any country which, upon the facts being disclosed, was found to be guilty of attempting to destroy what otherwise might be collective security. If that example were followed by other parts of the British Empire, as I believe it would be, it would soon be followed by other parts of the world.
I want to repeat these words:
Our country, small as it is, might well lay down a definite policy

That is my contention, Mr. Speaker, that this parliament should lay down a definite policy in regard to the very matters dealt with by the leader of the government as recently as April 1, 1935. That was a declared policy. So far we have seen nothing done to implement it. I well remember that last year,

in reference to this question, the right hon. gentleman informed me that an investigation would be launched in this country to find out the exact amount of profiteering, if there were any, going on in connection with arms and munitions manufactured in Canada. So far I have heard nothing as to the results of that investigation, if indeed it was carried out. That should be one of the very first steps we should take, and I think, as the right hon. gentleman mentioned in the quotation I gave a moment ago, this country could well take the lead in laying down the policy that we would not supply other countries with nickel or other material that might be used in the manufacture of arms and munitions.
Those are matters of vital importance to us. Day after day I receive resolutions. Not later than to-day I received a telegram advocating the abolition of trade with Japan. That is all well and good; I am not against a policy of barring trade, in connection with either imports from or exports to Japan, if that would be a cure-all. I well remember that at Christmas time in the store windows in western Canada we saw large placards bearing the words, "Boycott Japanese oranges." That would not stop the war. Our refusal to buy Japanese oranges in western Canada would not make any difference. If we refused to trade in commodities not essential to war it would make no difference at all. What we should concern ourselves with is the very thing we are neglecting, namely the making of armaments and munitions in Canada. Yet, of those commodities we export to the extent of about $1,000,000 a week, $52,000,000 a year, to Japan, and no step is taken to curtail that trade.
It is essential that one of the first steps to be taken this session-we should not wait until the next one-is to see that the export of arms and munitions from Canada is stopped. We are sending armaments to Japan and, although we hope not, we are almost certain that within a short time we are going to be sending our young men over there to be killed with the very ammunition we supply. Could there be anything more barbaric than that? Why do we not do something about it? We do nothing because capitalism steps in. Huge profits are made from the manufacture and sale of armaments and munitions. We permit this condition to exist, and we do not see fit to challenge it.
May I read an extract from the Canadian Unionist of December 17, dealing with profits and patriotism:
How the profit motive, the mainspring of capitalist enterprise, mocks patriotism is indicated by an article in Labour, official organ of the British Trades Union Congress. British

The Address-Mr. Johnston (Bow River)
armament firms are allowed to sell their productions to any and every customer-except Spam for the time being. They may sell to potential enemies. "Why should British firms arm our enemies?" the writer in Labour asks. He points out that there are not only obvious humanitarian and patriotic objections. The indiscriminate selling of arms leads to rivalry in armaments, thus tending to make wars more and more destructive. If a British firm supplies a submarine tc a foreign government, another government win' want destroyers to offset the menace of the submarine. So it goes; the more armaments supplied the greater the demand.
But capitalists want profits, and workers need jobs, and the inhuman, unpatriotic potentialities of the armament industry are a minor consideration. Governments permit the sale of arms to possible enemies because they say it helps to develop the country's armament industry, and the bigger that industry is the better a country is prepared for war.
. In a sane society, with production for use, instead of profit, the capital and labour now applied to the production of means of destruction would be utilized to supply better homes, better education, and better quality goods and services of all sorts.
That is the point. We talk about patriotism. If another war were declared we would preach patriotism to our young men. We would say, " Go out and fight for your homeland." Yes, we would tell them that; but we would not tell them at the same time that we have supplied the arms and ammunition to the enemy country; no, we would omit that. Our churches will broadcast patriotism throughout the country, but they, too, will omit that. When capitalism comes into contact with patriotism, capitalism wins every time.
I was deeply interested a few days ago in the observations made by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Howe) with respect to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. I do not criticize in every respect the actions of the corporation, because I believe in some respects they are commendable. I must say, too, that the type of program carried by the corporation is of a higher standard than those broadcast a while back. But while there are commendable features, there are features which should be criticized, and I can think of no better opportunity than the present to make the observations I have in mind.
Since announcing a fifty cent increase in the licence fees we have heard a great deal of criticism throughout Canada. True, there may be some wealthy men, like the Minister of Transport, who can afford three radios in their homes, or a radio for each member of their families. I wish them nothing but the best of success, and I trust they will be highly delighted with the entertainment they get. But unfortunately there are many people in this country who cannot afford three radios
in their homes. It is exceedingly difficult for people on relief or those about to be on relief to find that extra fifty cents. Not only is it an extra fifty cents in licence fee, but these people have to pay added costs in the form of maintenance charges and radio batteries. Those are charges which people in Ottawa do not have to bear, because the situation in eastern Canada is to some extent different from that in the west so far as electrical energy is concerned. In eastern Canada electricity costs about one and a half cents per kilowatt, whereas in the west it costs anywhere from eight cents to ten cents, with an extra meter charge of anywhere from ninety cents to a dollar and a half per month. Those are matters which have to be considered. The average set owner in the west cannot afford to have the extra burden placed upon him, and I think it is unfair to increase the fee at this time. I would have no objection to placing an extra fifty cent charge on a man who has a radio in his car. Further, I could see no objection to charging a man who has three radios in his house a fee for each set. That would be all right, because if a man can afford three radios he should be able to buy three licences for them.
On the other hand, to increase the fee on one set is entirely different. I find that the fifty cent increase per radio licence would bring in a total of about 8750,000. In view of the fact that not so long ago the broadcasting corporation advertised that they would have a surplus this year I would judge that with the increased revenue the total amount received would be about 82,780,000. I may be wrong in my figures, but I give them subject to correction. In view of the fact that they had a surplus last year and will have another S2,000.000 to spend this year, in the event of their doing as well in the coming year as they did in the last there would be no cause for complaint. But why is it necessary to raise the fee? That is something which has yet to be explained.
What was the reason for the increase? Was it pressure from somewhere? Probably the Department of Finance spoke again; probably an increased fee was demanded. Possibly political pressure was brought to bear, due to the loss of a few votes. However, that should not be a main consideration. May I point out that there is an interesting background to the announcement, one which was not revealed by the press. The announcement of the change was made following a closed meeting of newsnaper and
358	COMMONS
The Address-Mr. Johnston (Bow River)
magazine publishers with Mr. Gladstone Murray, General Manager of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. The meeting, convened in Toronto, was organized shortly after the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation had imported a number of outstanding radio programs originating in the United States. Or, to make the matter clearer, let me put it in this way:	The	Canadian Broadcasting
Corporation imports some United States programs; the newspaper and magazine publishers call a meeting which is attended by Mr. Gladstone Murray and then the licence fees are boosted.
The trade magazine, Broadcasting, in its edition of January 15, reports-and this report did not appear in the press-that both the magazin^ and newspaper publishers wanted to know how far the importation of United States programs was going to go. They claimed they were losing big advertising appropriations thereby. " Broadcasting " says it is understood that one publisher suggested that parliament be asked to grant the Canadian Broadcasting Commission a subsidy over a period of years so that commercial programs would not have to be broadcast by the Canadian Broadcasting Commission. In other words, the newspaper and magazine publishers want the government to bear the cost of broadcasting so that they will be able to get the money of the advertiser which now goes to pay for broadcasting. They want the cost of broadcasting to come out of the pockets of the people of Canada rather than out of the pockets of advertisers. Now, this is a significant paragraph, which appears in the January 15th edition of the weekly magazine Marketing, published in Toronto. Says the paragraph, referring to the Toronto meeting:
A constructive suggestion was made that if the Canadian Broadcasting Commission would seek to secure its needed additional revenue by increasing the licence fee on radio sets, the press would stand back of it and help the public realize that such increase was just and necessary; otherwise the press would have to consider the advisability of revealing what the Canadian Broadcasting Commission is doing in flooding Canada with United States programs.
Now, there you have not only a suggestion from the publishers to the Canadian Broadcasting Commission but a direct threat. The Canadian Broadcasting Commission must either boost radio licence fees or undergo a bombardment of newspaper criticism from coast to coast. But let the Canadian Broadcasting Commission boost the fee, and the press would use propaganda from coast to coast to prove to the people that the increase was necessary.

Well what happened? On January 19 an editorial on the subject appeared, for instance, in the Calgary Herald, and one paragraph read as follows:
The Herald is of the opinion that the radio corporation is on untenable ground in seeking to justify the importation of foreign advertising programs solely on the need of additional revenue. There is another obvious channel open to them which would not invite logical criticism now so freely voiced.
I pause to remark that we heard little criticism and much praise for the corporation when it imported the programs. However, to continue with the Herald's editorial:
The other obvious channel from which the corporation may obtain revenue is-by way of increasing the cost of each radio licence from $2 to $3. . . . By raising the fee one dollar, the net revenue on last year's basis would be increased to $2,780,000, a sum which should make the corporation independent of revenue from foreign advertising concerns.
That is the end of the quotation. It points to the attitude of the press-soak the people so that they, the publishers, can get their hands on the money of the advertisers.
The press, by its direct threat of criticism, placed the corporation in a most embarrassing position. By demanding that radio licence fees be increased, the publishers placed the corporation in the line of fire for criticism from every radio owner in Canada-the very people whom the corporation is called upon to serve; the people whose protests would do more than anything else to destroy the corporation. The publishers demanded an increase of $1. The corporation compromised and increased the licence fee by fifty cents.
There was a great deal of concern by the papers throughout Canada about the tremendous amount of United States broadcasting, but when one considers that only eight and a half hours, out of, I believe, ninety-eight hours, was thus being used, their protests are not impressive. Certainly there was not much complaint when it was first introduced; on the other hand everything in the line of praise was given to it; and when the corporation have selected, as I have said, some of the best types of United States programs, it seems curious that the press should take such great objection to this increased revenue. No, what they want is the money which was derived from that source. Here you have an example of the "freedom of the press" which was mentioned a moment ago. Who is controlling the country? The press. The only freedom they should have is the right to print the truth; that is as far as their freedom should go.
One other matter with regard to radio I do not think I can properly omit. In the west we have a different situation, perhaps, from

Privilege-Mr. Bennett
what prevails in the east, although the difference is not great. We are now asked to pay a fifty cent increase in the fee; but there is many a time out west, as well as in this city, when you turn on your radio and because of local interference you cannot hear anything. In fact the situation became so bad that a petition was sent to me from my constituency protesting against the interference, but no consideration is given as regards an adjustment of the fee. I had occasion to visit Calgary, where I was received very courteously by an official of the radio branch there-I believe it was Mr. Ainslie-with regard to this interference in radio. A trouble man was sent out to investigate the matter. He came out within a week after I visited the office, and made a thorough investigation of every radio concern in that town. He found that a great many machines were running without condensers, without means of eliminating this interference. He went around to each one of the firms, pointed out that this condition should be corrected, and told them how to do this. He then came around to my house and said he would return in one week. He did so, but things were just as bad. He made another round of the town and advised them again.
The point is this, that we are now paying fifty cents more for a licence; yet there is no regulation by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation or by this government which gives these trouble men authority to say to owners of machines which are interfering with reception, "You must change that or you will get into trouble", or "we will prosecute you." There is no regulation which directly covers this matter. These trouble men are much concerned about it, and I think properly so, and I should like to see the Minister of Transport provide by regulation that when they go to all the trouble and expense involved in checking up on interference they should be granted some authority whereby they can compel owners of machines which cause electrical interference to clear it up.
There is another question that I must mention. It has been referred to before, but it is of too great importance to be permitted to slip by as idly as has happened so far. I refer to the charges of political graft that were made not long ago in the house.
At 11.02 p.m. the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
